arguments object.summary: The arguments object is an array-like, iterable collection of every value supplied to a traditional function. It supports indexes and length, but not Array methods, and arrow functions inherit arguments from an enclosing normal function.
arguments object.explanation: Inside a traditional function, arguments exposes every value supplied at the call site through numeric indexes and length. It is iterable and array-like, but it is not an Array, so convert it before using array methods. Arrow functions do not create their own arguments object.

example.title: Read all supplied arguments
example.explanation: Converts the array-like object to an array, then sums every supplied argument.

useCases.title: Variadic functions
useCases.scenario: Accepting a variable number of values in legacy or interop code.

useCases.title: Argument counting
useCases.scenario: Inspecting how many values a caller supplied.

useCases.title: Dynamic argument processing
useCases.scenario: Iterating over caller-supplied values in a traditional function.

keyPoints: A traditional function can inspect every supplied argument through numeric indexes.
Use arguments.length to count how many values the caller supplied.
The object is iterable, so it can be traversed with for...of.
Treat arguments as array-like rather than as a true Array.
Convert arguments to an Array before calling Array methods.
It includes values even when the function declaration has fewer named parameters.
gotchas: arguments has indexes and length, but it does not provide Array methods such as map or reduce.
Arrow functions do not have their own arguments object; an arguments reference resolves to an enclosing normal function.
Unlike rest parameters, arguments cannot capture only a selected portion of the supplied values.

Array flattening.summary: Use flat() to create a new array with nested arrays concatenated to a chosen depth. Use flatMap() when transforming elements and flattening the results by one level in one operation.
Array flattening.explanation: JavaScript provides flat() for depth-controlled flattening and flatMap() for mapping each element followed by one-level flattening. Both return new arrays rather than modifying the original array.

parameters.name: depth
parameters.description: Maximum nesting depth to flatten; defaults to 1. A larger value allows deeper nested arrays to be concatenated.

parameters.name: callbackFn
parameters.description: Function called for each present array element; its returned arrays are flattened one level.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional value used as this when callbackFn executes.

Array flattening.returns: flat() returns a new array with nested array elements concatenated through the requested depth. flatMap() returns a new array containing callback results flattened by one level.

example.title: Flatten nested arrays
example.explanation: Use flat() to copy an array while concatenating nested arrays to a chosen depth; use flatMap() when mapping and flattening one level belong together.

useCases.title: Normalize nested data
useCases.scenario: A collection contains arrays nested one or more levels deep and needs a new, shallower array.

useCases.title: Map and expand items
useCases.scenario: Each input element should produce zero, one, or several output elements.

useCases.title: Simplify flattening code
useCases.scenario: A legacy reduce-and-concat flattening expression should be replaced by the built-in operation.

interview.question: What does Array.prototype.flat() do?
interview.answer: flat() returns a new array and concatenates nested arrays recursively up to the supplied depth. With no argument, the depth is 1.
interview.followUp: What happens with deeper nesting? Call flat() with a larger depth, such as Infinity, to continue through all nested levels.

interview.question: How does flatMap() differ from map().flat()?
interview.answer: flatMap() applies a callback to each present element and then flattens the callback results by exactly one level. It combines the usual map(...).flat(1) operation.
interview.followUp: Can the callback return a scalar? Yes; only returned arrays are flattened, while scalar results become ordinary elements.

interview.question: Do flat() and flatMap() mutate the original array?
interview.answer: Neither method mutates the receiver. flat() produces a shallow copied result, while flatMap() creates a new array containing mapped results flattened one level.
interview.followUp: What does flat() do to sparse arrays? It removes empty slots at the levels being flattened.

keyPoints: flat() is non-mutating: it constructs and returns a separate array.
The depth argument controls how many nested array levels are concatenated.
Calling flat() without an argument flattens one level.
flatMap() transforms each element with a callback before flattening the callback output.
flatMap() always performs only one flattening level.
Conceptually, flatMap(callback) is equivalent to array.map(callback).flat(1).
gotchas: Sparse-array holes are removed at the levels that flat() processes, so flattening can change the positions and length of elements.
Only actual nested arrays are flattened; other values remain unchanged.
flatMap() skips holes in its source array because its mapping callback is not invoked for empty slots.

Array holes.summary: Array holes are missing indexed properties, not stored undefined values. They make an array sparse, and different operations either skip the missing positions or expose them as undefined.
Array holes.explanation: An array hole is an absent indexed property, not an element whose value is undefined. Holes can arise from omitted literal entries, Array(length), or assigning beyond the current end; some operations treat them as undefined, while many array iteration methods skip them.
Array holes.syntax:
const sparse = [value, , value];
const empty = Array(length);

example.title: Distinguishing an array hole from undefined
example.code:
const holes = [1, , 3];
const undefinedValue = [1, undefined, 3];

console.log(holes.length); // 3
console.log(holes[1]); // undefined
console.log(holes.hasOwnProperty(1)); // false
console.log(undefinedValue.hasOwnProperty(1)); // true

holes.forEach((value) => console.log(value)); // 1, 3
for (const value of holes) console.log(value); // 1, undefined, 3
example.explanation: A hole has no property at its index, although indexed access produces undefined. Array iteration methods such as forEach skip holes, while for...of visits the position as undefined.

useCases.title: Detecting missing elements
useCases.scenario: Testing whether an index is present rather than merely reading as undefined.

useCases.title: Reasoning about iteration
useCases.scenario: Predicting callback counts and results when processing partially populated arrays.

useCases.title: Constructing sparse arrays
useCases.scenario: Representing index ranges with intentionally uninitialized positions.

interview.question: How does a hole differ from an explicit undefined element?
interview.answer: A hole is a missing indexed property, whereas an explicit undefined value is an existing property containing undefined. Both usually produce undefined through indexed access, but hasOwnProperty or the in operator distinguishes them.
interview.followUp: What happens with for...of? It visits the hole position and yields undefined, unlike forEach, which skips the missing property.

interview.question: How can sparse arrays be created?
interview.answer: An array literal can omit an element between commas, such as [1, , 3]. Array(5) creates five empty slots, and assigning a far index creates holes between the old end and that index.
interview.followUp: Why can a far index be surprising? It increases length to the assigned index plus one while leaving intervening indices absent.

interview.question: Which operations skip holes, and which observe their positions?
interview.answer: Indexed access and for...of expose holes as undefined-like values, while forEach and map skip them. Therefore, array length does not indicate how many callbacks an iteration method will make.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect actual present indices? Object.keys lists only existing properties, whereas Array.prototype.keys iterates every index position.

keyPoints: An array containing one or more holes is sparse; an array with every index populated is dense.
Extra trailing commas can create holes, so punctuation that looks harmless may change the array's structure.
A literal with omitted entries creates holes while preserving those positions in the array's length.
forEach and map omit holes rather than passing undefined to their callbacks.
The observable result depends on the operation: indexed reads and some iteration forms expose a hole as undefined.
gotchas: Consecutive commas in an array literal or the Array constructor can create holes; assigning an index beyond the current length also creates intervening empty slots.
Do not assume a hole and an explicit undefined value are interchangeable: the index is absent in the first case but present in the second.
Methods such as forEach and map do not invoke their callbacks for holes, so callback counts can be smaller than array length.

Array.from iterables.summary: Array.from turns an iterable or array-like value into a real array. It can also transform each item while building that array.
Array.from iterables.explanation: Array.from takes an iterable or array-like value, creates a new ordinary array, and copies its elements in iteration order. An optional mapping function can transform each element during creation, with an optional thisArg supplying its this value.

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: An iterable or array-like value to convert into a real array.

parameters.name: mapFn
parameters.description: Optional function applied to each element before it is added.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional this value used while mapFn runs.

Array.from iterables.returns: A new, ordinary Array containing the copied values.

example.title: Convert iterables and map values
example.explanation: Converts a string and a Set into ordinary arrays; the mapping function transforms each Set value before it is added.

useCases.title: Normalize iterable data
useCases.scenario: Convert strings, Sets, Maps, generators, or other iterable values before using array methods.

useCases.title: Convert and transform
useCases.scenario: Create a transformed array in one operation with the optional mapping callback.

useCases.title: Handle array-like values
useCases.scenario: Convert array-like objects such as indexed collections into ordinary arrays.

interview.question: What does Array.from do?
interview.answer: Array.from creates a new real Array from an iterable or array-like object. For an iterable, it reads values through the iterable protocol and places them into the new array.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from spread syntax? Array.from supports array-like objects as well as iterables, whereas spread syntax only supports iterables.

interview.question: What are Array.from's optional arguments?
interview.answer: The second argument is mapFn, which runs for every source element before that element is inserted into the result. The third argument, thisArg, sets the this value used by mapFn.
interview.followUp: Why use Array.from with mapFn instead of calling map afterward? It performs conversion and transformation in one creation step, avoiding a separate mapping pass.

interview.question: What does Array.from return, and does it create sparse arrays?
interview.answer: Array.from returns a new Array instance and does not mutate the source. It also produces a dense array, so absent indexed properties become undefined rather than holes.
interview.followUp: What should be used for an async iterable? Use Array.fromAsync, which is specifically documented for asynchronous iteration.

keyPoints: It is useful for turning iterable data into a normal array so array methods can be used.
The operation creates a separate result and copies source items into it.
mapFn transforms each value during construction, before insertion into the output.
thisArg controls the receiver seen by the mapping function.
A custom value qualifies as an iterable when it supplies Symbol.iterator.
gotchas: Missing indexed properties are represented as undefined rather than leaving holes in the resulting array.
Array.from is synchronous and is not the choice for consuming asynchronous iterables.

Array.prototype.sort default.summary: Array.prototype.sort() rearranges an array in place and returns the same array. Without a comparator, it compares string representations by UTF-16 code units, so numeric values require an explicit numeric comparator.
Array.prototype.sort default.explanation: Calling sort() rearranges the existing array and returns that same array. With no comparator, defined elements are converted to strings and compared by UTF-16 code units, so numeric-looking values may sort lexicographically rather than numerically; undefined elements go last.

parameters.name: compareFn
parameters.description: Optional comparator receiving two elements and returning a negative, positive, or zero number to determine their order.

Array.prototype.sort default.returns: The same array reference, after its elements have been sorted.

example.title: Default lexicographic sort
example.explanation: Without a comparator, numeric values are compared as strings; provide a numeric comparator for ascending numeric order.

useCases.title: Numeric ordering with a comparator
useCases.scenario: You need a list ordered by numeric value.

useCases.title: Non-mutating sorting with toSorted()
useCases.scenario: You need a sorted result while preserving the input array.

useCases.title: Stable ordering
useCases.scenario: You need deterministic ordering for records with equal sort keys.

interview.question: What is surprising about the default ordering of numbers?
interview.answer: With no argument, sort converts non-undefined elements to strings and compares their UTF-16 code units. Therefore, [10, 2, 1] sorts as [1, 10, 2], not numeric ascending order.
interview.followUp: How would you sort numbers ascending? Pass (a, b) => a - b as the comparator.

interview.question: Does sort() mutate the original array?
interview.answer: The method sorts the array in place and returns a reference to that same, now-sorted array. It does not produce an independent array.
interview.followUp: How can you avoid mutation? Use toSorted(), which returns a sorted copy.

interview.question: What contract does a compare function follow?
interview.answer: A comparator receives two elements and should return a negative number when the first belongs before the second, a positive number when it belongs after it, or zero when their order is equivalent. Omitting it selects the string-based default.
interview.followUp: What happens to undefined elements with a comparator? They are placed at the end without calling the comparator for them.

keyPoints: No comparator means ascending lexicographic ordering after conversion to strings.
String comparison uses UTF-16 code-unit sequences, not numeric magnitude.
Use toSorted() when the original array must remain unchanged.
Equal-comparison elements preserve their original relative order in modern JavaScript.
gotchas: The default is not numeric sorting: values are stringified and ordered lexicographically.
undefined values always move to the end, and the comparator is not called for them.

Arrow function this.summary: Arrow functions do not have their own `this`; they read it from the surrounding context. This makes them useful as callbacks inside methods when the callback must preserve the method's object context.
Arrow function this.explanation: An arrow function does not create its own `this`. When it uses `this`, JavaScript looks outward to the enclosing lexical environment, so the value comes from the surrounding regular function or method rather than from the way the arrow callback is invoked.

example.title: Arrow callback preserves the surrounding this
example.explanation: The callback is an arrow function, so it reads `this` from `showList()` and preserves the object context.

useCases.title: Preserve method context
useCases.scenario: A callback inside an object method needs to access the method's object context.

useCases.title: Concise callbacks
useCases.scenario: A small callback should use surrounding state without manually binding a regular function.

useCases.title: Non-constructor functions
useCases.scenario: A function should intentionally reject constructor-style invocation.

interview.question: How does `this` differ in an arrow callback and a regular callback?
interview.answer: Arrow functions do not have their own `this`; they obtain it from the surrounding lexical environment. Therefore, a callback arrow inside an object method can use the method's `this` without losing the object context.
interview.followUp: What happens if `call()` supplies another context? The arrow ignores that attempted context because its `this` is determined outside the arrow.

interview.question: When is an arrow function useful inside an object method?
interview.answer: A regular function gets `this` according to how it is called, while an arrow function takes `this` from outside. This makes arrows useful when a callback should preserve the surrounding method context.
interview.followUp: Why not use an arrow for every method? A method often needs its caller-dependent `this`, which an arrow cannot provide.

interview.question: What limitations follow from an arrow function's missing `this`?
interview.answer: Arrow functions have no own `this`, `arguments`, or constructor behavior. They also cannot be called with `new`, so they are intended for functions and callbacks rather than constructor roles.
interview.followUp: What other function feature is absent? Arrow functions also do not provide their own `arguments` variable; they use the enclosing scope's one.

keyPoints: An arrow function does not define a new `this` binding.
A `this` reference inside an arrow resolves through the enclosing scope.
An arrow callback in `forEach` can directly reuse the surrounding method's `this`.
In the documented pattern, the callback can reach the containing object's `title` through the inherited context.
The missing own `this` is part of a broader limitation: arrows also lack a local `arguments` binding.
gotchas: An arrow function cannot be invoked with `new`, so it cannot serve as a constructor.
An arrow function cannot receive a method-style `this`; using it as an object method will not make `this` refer to that object.
An arrow function is not equivalent to calling `bind(this)`: it closes over the outer `this` instead of creating a separately bound function.

async await ordering.summary: async functions return promises, and await pauses only the surrounding function. After the awaited promise settles, execution continues asynchronously through the microtask queue, so caller code and other microtasks can run first.
async await ordering.explanation: An async function starts running immediately, but await pauses that function and returns control to its caller. Once the awaited promise settles, the suspended continuation is scheduled as a microtask, so statements after await run after currently executing synchronous code and already queued microtasks.
async await ordering.returns: An async function always returns a Promise; non-promise return values are wrapped automatically.

example.title: Execution resumes after await
example.explanation: The function runs synchronously through the await, then resumes asynchronously; the caller's next synchronous statement runs first.

useCases.title: Dependent async steps
useCases.scenario: Read sequential asynchronous results where each step depends on the previous one.

useCases.title: Readable error handling
useCases.scenario: Handle promise failures with ordinary try/catch control flow.

useCases.title: Concurrent promise coordination
useCases.scenario: Coordinate several independent operations with Promise.all.

interview.question: Why does code after await run later?
interview.answer: An async function begins synchronously until it reaches await. At that point it yields to its caller, and the code after await resumes in a microtask after the awaited value settles.
interview.followUp: What happens with an already-resolved promise? The continuation is still deferred, and other already-scheduled microtasks are processed first.

interview.question: Does await block the whole program?
interview.answer: await pauses the surrounding async function rather than blocking JavaScript globally. Caller code and other independent asynchronous work can continue while the promise is pending.
interview.followUp: How can two operations start concurrently? Create both promises before awaiting them, then await Promise.all on the group.

interview.question: What does async change about a function's return value?
interview.answer: async guarantees that the function returns a promise; ordinary returned values are automatically wrapped as fulfilled promises. A rejection from the awaited promise propagates as an exception unless handled.
interview.followUp: How should multiple independent promises be coordinated? Use Promise.all when all results are required, rather than awaiting them one by one.

keyPoints: Every async function call produces a promise, even when the function returns an ordinary value.
await unwraps the fulfilled result and suspends the surrounding async function until settlement.
Promise.all is the documented composition pattern for awaiting several promises together.

async generators.summary: Async generators produce sequences lazily while allowing asynchronous work between values. Declare them with `async function*` and consume them using `for await...of`.
async generators.explanation: An async generator combines generator-style lazy production with asynchronous operations. Declare it with `async function*`, use `yield` to produce values, and consume the returned async iterable with `for await...of`; calls to `next()` produce promises.
async generators.returns: The generator function returns an asynchronous iterable whose `next()` method returns promises.

example.title: Yield values asynchronously
example.explanation: The loop asynchronously consumes each value produced by the generator.

useCases.title: Process asynchronous streams
useCases.scenario: Data arrives over time, such as network responses or delayed events.

useCases.title: Generate values on demand
useCases.scenario: A producer should avoid creating all results before the consumer requests them.

useCases.title: Coordinate asynchronous steps
useCases.scenario: A sequence requires `await` between yielded values.

interview.question: How do you declare an async generator, and what does calling it return?
interview.answer: Declare an async generator with `async function*`. It can use both `await` for asynchronous work and `yield` for lazy value production, and calling it returns an async iterable object.
interview.followUp: How should its output be consumed? Use `for await...of`, which waits for each asynchronously produced value.

interview.question: What does `next()` return on an async generator?
interview.answer: Each call to `next()` is asynchronous and returns a promise. The promise eventually provides the iterator result for the next yielded value.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful for streaming? It lets production and consumption proceed on demand as asynchronous data becomes available.

interview.question: When would you choose an async generator?
interview.answer: Async generators are useful when a sequence arrives asynchronously, such as data downloaded in chunks. They allow asynchronous operations inside the generator while preserving generator-style iteration.
interview.followUp: What syntax replaces synchronous iteration? Use `for await...of` rather than `for...of`.

keyPoints: Write `async function*` to create an async generator function.
The `async` modifier changes the generator so its iteration proceeds asynchronously.
Its body can await delays, promises, and network operations before yielding values.
Consume the returned async iterable with a `for await...of` loop.
Choose async generators when sequence elements become available asynchronously.
gotchas: Treating `next()` as returning an iterator result immediately is incorrect; it returns a promise.
Use `for await...of`, not ordinary `for...of`, when consuming an async iterable.

Autoboxing.summary: JavaScript primitives can use methods because the language temporarily wraps them in corresponding objects. The primitive remains unchanged; null and undefined are exceptions.
Autoboxing.explanation: When a property or method is accessed on a primitive, JavaScript can create a temporary wrapper object such as String, Number, or Boolean. The operation uses that wrapper, which is then discarded, so the original value remains a primitive. null and undefined are exceptions because they have no corresponding wrappers.

example.title: Primitive method access
example.explanation: The string remains a primitive even though JavaScript lets it use methods through a temporary wrapper.

useCases.title: String processing
useCases.scenario: Call string methods such as toUpperCase() without manually converting a string to a String object.

useCases.title: Number formatting
useCases.scenario: Use number methods such as toFixed() while retaining a numeric primitive.

useCases.title: Debugging primitive properties
useCases.scenario: Understand why primitive values do not retain custom properties assigned through temporary wrappers.

keyPoints: Primitive values can use methods such as toUpperCase() and toFixed(), even though they are not objects.
Method access is modeled as creating a temporary wrapper around the primitive and discarding it afterward.
String, Number, Boolean, Symbol, and BigInt primitives have corresponding wrapper types.
Using a string method does not change the string into an object; the value remains primitive.
Wrapper creation is a language model, and engines optimize it so ordinary primitive method calls are inexpensive.
Temporary-wrapper semantics explain primitive methods without implying a persistent object allocation.
gotchas: Do not call methods or access properties on null or undefined; they have no wrapper objects and cause an error.
Avoid explicitly constructing wrapper objects with new String(), new Number(), or new Boolean(); use primitive values instead.

BigInt arithmetic.summary: BigInt is JavaScript’s integer type for values of arbitrary length. Its arithmetic resembles Number arithmetic, but operands cannot be mixed with regular numbers and division truncates toward zero.
BigInt arithmetic.explanation: BigInt values represent integers of arbitrary length. Create them with an n suffix or BigInt(), then use matching BigInt operands for arithmetic; division rounds toward zero and produces another BigInt.
BigInt arithmetic.returns: Arithmetic expressions involving BigInts return BigInt values.

example.title: BigInt arithmetic
example.explanation: BigInt operands support arithmetic, and division discards the fractional part by rounding toward zero.

useCases.title: Large integer arithmetic
useCases.scenario: Calculating exact integer values beyond Number’s safe precision range.

useCases.title: Whole-number division
useCases.scenario: Performing integer division where fractional results are intentionally discarded.

useCases.title: Parsing large integers
useCases.scenario: Representing large integer quantities received as strings or other supported inputs.

interview.question: What is BigInt and how is it created?
interview.answer: BigInt is a numeric type for integers of arbitrary length. It can be created with an integer literal followed by n or with BigInt().
interview.followUp: How does BigInt division differ from Number division? It rounds toward zero and removes the fractional part.

interview.question: Can BigInt and Number values be mixed in arithmetic?
interview.answer: Arithmetic operands must use the same numeric type, so a BigInt cannot be directly combined with a regular Number. Explicitly convert with BigInt() or Number() when mixing is required.
interview.followUp: Why is explicit conversion preferred? It makes the intended result type clear and avoids implicit precision-related surprises.

interview.question: What does BigInt division return?
interview.answer: BigInt arithmetic returns BigInt values, including division. Division rounds toward zero, so 5n / 2n evaluates to 2n rather than a fractional value.
interview.followUp: What happens when converting the result to Number()? The value becomes a Number, and large integers can lose precision.

keyPoints: BigInt is intended for integer calculations whose values may exceed ordinary number precision.
An integer literal becomes BigInt by adding the n suffix.
The BigInt() function can construct a BigInt from supported string or number inputs.
Common arithmetic operators work with BigInt operands in much the same way as with ordinary numbers.
BigInt arithmetic preserves the BigInt result type.
gotchas: Arithmetic cannot combine BigInt and Number operands directly; convert one operand explicitly first.
Do not use unary plus as a BigInt conversion; use Number() when a number is required.

Bitwise Tricks.summary: JavaScript bitwise operators manipulate the binary representation of 32-bit integer operands. They include logical bit operations and left or right shifts, and are mainly useful for specialized low-level tasks.
Bitwise Tricks.explanation: JavaScript bitwise operators convert numeric operands to 32-bit integers and apply the operation to their binary representations. AND, OR, XOR, and NOT manipulate corresponding bits, while shift operators move bits left or right; the result is an ordinary JavaScript number.
Bitwise Tricks.syntax: a & b; a | b; a ^ b; ~a; a << b; a >> b; a >>> b
Bitwise Tricks.returns: Each operator produces a JavaScript number resulting from its bitwise operation.

useCases.title: Low-level algorithms
useCases.scenario: Implementing specialized low-level numeric or cryptographic algorithms.

keyPoints: Bitwise operators work on 32-bit integer representations rather than directly on decimal values.
The available operators are AND (&), OR (|), XOR (^), NOT (~), left shift (<<), right shift (>>), and zero-fill right shift (>>>).
The same family of bitwise operators is common across many programming languages.
Bitwise syntax and concepts are broadly shared, which can help when translating low-level algorithms between languages.
Bitwise operations can be appropriate in specialized areas such as cryptography.
gotchas: Operands are handled as 32-bit integers, so bitwise operations are unsuitable when preserving arbitrary-precision numeric values matters.

Block Scope.summary: `const` creates a block-scoped binding that must be initialized immediately and cannot be reassigned. The referenced object or array may still be mutated.
Block Scope.explanation: A `const` declaration creates a binding available only within its containing block, function, or module. The binding must be initialized when declared, cannot be reassigned, and cannot be accessed before its declaration is reached because it is in the temporal dead zone. If it refers to an object or array, the binding stays fixed while the referenced contents may still change.

useCases.scenario: Keep a binding from being reassigned after setup.

useCases.title: Block-local variables
useCases.scenario: Limit temporary names to a branch or loop body.

useCases.title: Mutable object state
useCases.scenario: Share a stable reference while updating object contents.

interview.question: How does `const` differ from `var` regarding block scope?
interview.answer: `const` is block-scoped, so a binding declared inside braces is unavailable outside them. A nested declaration with the same name is a separate binding and can shadow an outer one.
interview.followUp: What happens with `var` in the same block? `var` is not block-scoped; it belongs to the containing function or script instead.

interview.question: Why must a `const` declaration be initialized immediately?
interview.answer: A `const` binding must receive an initializer in its declaration. It cannot later be assigned a value, because reassignment of the binding is disallowed.
interview.followUp: Can `const x;` be made valid? No; unlike an uninitialized `let`, a `const` declaration without an initializer is invalid.

interview.question: What is the temporal dead zone for `const`?
interview.answer: The declaration is in the temporal dead zone from the beginning of its scope until initialization is processed. Accessing it during that interval throws a `ReferenceError`.
interview.followUp: Does placing the declaration later permit an earlier read? No; the binding exists for scope analysis, but it is inaccessible until execution reaches initialization.

keyPoints: A `const` binding is local to its surrounding block, function, or module rather than being generally visible throughout the program.
Assignment cannot replace the value held by a `const` binding after initialization.
Object and array contents remain mutable unless the referenced value is separately protected.
A top-level script `const` does not become a property of the global object.
`const` must appear in a declaration form; it cannot be used as a standalone statement body.
gotchas: `const` prevents reassignment of the binding, not mutation of an object or array referenced by that binding.
Reading a `const` before its declaration throws a `ReferenceError`; moving the declaration later does not make the earlier read valid.
A second declaration using the same name in one scope is an error, although a nested block may declare a shadowing binding.

Boolean coercion.summary: JavaScript coerces values to booleans in conditions and other Boolean contexts. Only a small set of values is falsy; every other value is truthy.
Boolean coercion.explanation: JavaScript converts values to booleans whenever an operation requires a Boolean, including conditions and loops. The falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN, and document.all; every other value is truthy. Boolean(value) or !!value performs the same conversion explicitly.
Boolean coercion.returns: A Boolean primitive when conversion is explicitly requested with Boolean(value) or !!value; Boolean contexts use the converted result for their operation.

useCases.title: Defaulting and conditional selection
useCases.scenario: Use short-circuit expressions to select values based on their truthiness.

interview.question: What is Boolean coercion?
interview.answer: JavaScript applies Boolean coercion in Boolean contexts such as conditionals and loops. Values such as false, 0, an empty string, null, undefined, and NaN become false; other values become true.
interview.followUp: How can coercion be made explicit? Use Boolean(value) or the double-NOT operator !!value; both produce a Boolean primitive.

interview.question: Which values are falsy?
interview.answer: The falsy set includes false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN, and document.all. Every other JavaScript value is truthy.
interview.followUp: Is [] falsy because it is empty? No. Arrays and other objects are truthy, regardless of whether they contain elements.

interview.question: Does a logical operator always return true or false?
interview.answer: Logical operators use truthiness but do not necessarily return a Boolean. For example, && returns the first falsy operand, or the last operand when all operands are truthy.
interview.followUp: What does || return? It returns the first truthy operand, or the final operand if all operands are falsy.

keyPoints: Conditions and loops automatically convert their tested expressions to Boolean values.
Only the documented falsy values convert to false; all other values convert to true.
Boolean(value) is an explicit way to obtain a Boolean primitive.
&& uses truthiness for control flow and returns an operand rather than necessarily returning true or false.
gotchas: An empty array or object is truthy, even though it may appear empty.

Chained optional calls.summary: Optional chaining safely accesses nested properties and optionally calls methods when an intermediate value may be null or undefined. A nullish value before ?. short-circuits the remaining chain and returns undefined.
Chained optional calls.explanation: Optional chaining places ?. at a property access, computed access, or function call that may be absent. If the value on its left is null or undefined, evaluation stops and the complete expression produces undefined; otherwise, the access or call proceeds normally.
Chained optional calls.returns: The accessed value or function result when the chain succeeds; otherwise undefined when an optional link encounters null or undefined.

example.title: Safely access nested data and an optional method
example.explanation: Each optional link checks the value immediately before it and stops the remaining chain when that value is nullish.

useCases.title: Nullable nested data
useCases.scenario: Read deeply nested configuration or API data whose intermediate objects may be absent.

useCases.title: Optional callbacks
useCases.scenario: Invoke an optional callback or method without first writing an explicit existence check.

useCases.title: Computed property access
useCases.scenario: Access a dynamically named property when the container itself may be missing.

interview.question: What does optional chaining do when the checked value is nullish?
interview.answer: It checks the value immediately to the left of ?. and stops if that value is null or undefined. The expression then evaluates to undefined instead of throwing for that optional step.
interview.followUp: What happens with user?.profile.name? Only user is optional; if user exists but profile is nullish, .name is still unsafe.

interview.question: What are the three documented forms of optional chaining?
interview.answer: The property form is obj?.prop, the computed form is obj?.[prop], and the optional-call form is obj.method?.(). The call form invokes the method only when that property exists.
interview.followUp: Why use method?.() rather than obj?.method()? The former checks whether the method is callable at that property; the latter first checks obj and then performs a normal property access.

interview.question: How does short-circuiting affect chained evaluation?
interview.answer: Optional chaining short-circuits later work in the same chain when the left side is undefined or null. Function calls or other operations to its right are not performed after that short circuit.
interview.followUp: What should be verified in code review? Ensure each potentially absent intermediate value has an optional marker and that silently returning undefined is acceptable.

keyPoints: A nullish value immediately before ?. ends the chain and yields undefined.
When the base value exists, optional property access behaves like ordinary dot access.
Use bracket form when the property name comes from an expression.
An optional call skips invocation when the method is missing.
Repeated optional links allow nested property traversal without separate null checks.
Short-circuiting also prevents later calls and operations in the same chain.
gotchas: Optional chaining does not make an undeclared identifier safe; referencing one still causes a ReferenceError.
Every potentially missing link needs its own ?. marker; one optional access does not protect later ordinary accesses.
Do not use it when absence should be treated as an error, because it silently converts the missing value into undefined.

Closures.sourceTitle: Variable scope, closure - The Modern JavaScript Tutorial
Closures.summary: Closures let functions retain access to variables from the lexical environment where they were created. This supports persistent state, private data, and callbacks that run after their surrounding function has finished.
Closures.explanation: A closure is a function together with the lexical environment where it was created. JavaScript functions retain a reference to that environment, allowing them to read or change outer variables later; variable lookup proceeds from the current environment outward through the scope chain.
Closures.syntax: function outer() { const value = ...; return function inner() { ...value... }; }

example.title: A private counter
example.explanation: The returned function keeps access to `count` after `makeCounter` has finished, so each call updates the same private variable.

useCases.title: Encapsulation
useCases.scenario: Keep mutable state private behind a returned function.

useCases.title: Callbacks
useCases.scenario: Preserve context for callbacks executed later.

useCases.title: Function factories
useCases.scenario: Build configurable functions by capturing setup values.

interview.question: What is a closure?
interview.answer: A closure combines a function with the lexical environment in which that function was created. The function can later access variables from that environment even after the surrounding call has returned.
interview.followUp: What determines which variable is read when several scopes use the same name? Lookup starts in the innermost environment and continues outward, so the nearest binding wins.

interview.question: How can a closure preserve private state?
interview.answer: Each function call creates a new lexical environment for its parameters and local variables. A returned inner function retains the relevant environment, which lets separate calls maintain separate captured state.
interview.followUp: Why do two counters made by the same factory not share state? Each factory call creates a distinct environment, and each returned function closes over its own environment.

interview.question: Why can closures in loops produce unexpected values?
interview.answer: `let` and `const` create block-level bindings, while `var` is scoped to the current function or script. In a loop, block-scoped bindings can give iterations distinct captured values; `var` commonly leaves callbacks sharing one binding.
interview.followUp: How can the `var` loop issue be avoided? Use `let` for the loop variable or create a separate scope for each iteration.

keyPoints: Functions, blocks, and scripts each have an associated lexical environment that stores bindings and links to an outer environment.
A lexical environment contains an environment record for local bindings plus a reference to its outer lexical environment.
Calling a function creates a fresh environment for that invocation’s parameters and local variables.
JavaScript functions are closures by default, although many do not visibly capture useful outer state.
A closure allows code in a function to access variables from enclosing scopes.
Variable resolution follows the scope chain from the current environment toward the global environment.
gotchas: A function remembers the environment from its creation site, not the location where it is eventually called.
Name lookup checks the nearest environment first, so an inner declaration can shadow an outer variable.

Comma in arrays.summary: A trailing comma after the last item in an array literal is allowed and ignored. It keeps multiline array edits consistent, but additional commas create sparse-array holes.
Comma in arrays.explanation: A trailing comma may appear after the last item in a JavaScript array literal. It does not create another element, and it can make multiline edits easier because each item line has the same format.

example.title: Trailing comma in an array
example.code:
const fruits = [
  "Apple",
  "Orange",
  "Plum",
];

console.log(fruits.length); // 3
console.log(fruits[2]); // "Plum"
example.explanation: The final comma is ignored, so the array contains three elements.

useCases.title: Keep item lines uniform
useCases.scenario: Formatting multiline arrays

useCases.title: Make additions produce smaller diffs
useCases.scenario: Maintaining source code

useCases.title: Distinguish one trailing comma from extra commas
useCases.scenario: Avoiding accidental sparse arrays

keyPoints: Array literals support a comma after their final element.
A single final comma does not increase the array's length or add an element.
In multiline arrays, trailing commas make adding or removing entries simpler and produce cleaner diffs.
Multiple final commas create missing array slots rather than additional ordinary elements.
gotchas: Do not add multiple commas after the final item: the extra comma creates a sparse-array hole.
A hole is not the same as an explicit undefined value; common iteration methods skip it.

Comma Operator.summary: The comma operator evaluates several expressions from left to right and returns only the last expression's value. Parentheses are often needed because comma has very low precedence.
Comma Operator.explanation: The comma operator evaluates expressions from left to right and produces the value of the final expression. Earlier results are discarded, so those expressions are useful mainly when they cause side effects; parentheses are often required because the operator has very low precedence.

parameters.name: expressions
parameters.description: Expressions evaluated from left to right; the final expression determines the compound expression's value.

Comma Operator.returns: The value of the last expression.

example.title: Evaluation and multiple loop updates
example.explanation: The first expression runs for its side effect, while the parenthesized expression evaluates to the final value. The loop uses the operator to update two variables.

useCases.title: Multiple for-loop updates
useCases.scenario: A loop must update more than one variable after each iteration.

useCases.title: Compact side-effect expression
useCases.scenario: Earlier expressions need to run while one final value is required.

interview.question: What does the comma operator return?
interview.answer: It evaluates each operand from left to right, then returns the value of the last operand. Values produced by earlier operands are discarded.
interview.followUp: What happens in `(x++, x)`? `x++` runs first, then the updated value of `x` is returned by the second operand.

interview.question: Why can parentheses be necessary with the comma operator?
interview.answer: Its precedence is lower than assignment, so `a = 1, 2` is grouped as `(a = 1), 2`. To assign the final result of the comma expression, write `a = (1, 2)`.
interview.followUp: Why does `a = (1, 2)` assign `2`? Parentheses force the comma expression to be evaluated before assignment.

interview.question: Where is the comma operator commonly useful?
interview.answer: A common use is putting multiple update expressions in a `for` loop, such as `i++, j--`. The updates run left to right after each iteration.
interview.followUp: What must earlier operands generally provide to be useful? They should normally have side effects, such as assignments, calls, or increment operations.

keyPoints: It combines multiple expressions into one expression.
All operands run in left-to-right order, but only the final operand supplies the expression's value.
Earlier operand results do not survive; use them for effects rather than their values.
The operator binds very loosely, making grouping parentheses important in larger expressions.
Its unusual, limited role makes explicit statements preferable when they express the same logic more clearly.
gotchas: Because comma binds more weakly than assignment, parenthesize a comma expression when assigning its final result.
It is uncommon outside compact control-flow code, so separate statements may be clearer when no single expression is required.

computed property names.sourceTitle: Object initializer - JavaScript | MDN Web Docs
computed property names.summary: Computed property names let object literals derive keys from evaluated expressions. Put the expression in square brackets to create a dynamic property name.
computed property names.explanation: In an object initializer, place an expression inside square brackets to compute a property key. JavaScript evaluates that expression and uses its result as the key, enabling names derived from variables, concatenation, or other runtime values.

example.title: Build object keys from expressions
example.explanation: Expressions in square brackets are evaluated to create the object’s property names.

useCases.title: Dynamic configuration keys
useCases.scenario: A configuration object needs keys based on a variable such as a field name.

useCases.title: Generated naming conventions
useCases.scenario: An object needs consistently formatted keys assembled from prefixes, capitalization, or suffixes.

useCases.title: Computed method names
useCases.scenario: An object literal needs a method whose name is calculated from an expression.

interview.question: What is a computed property name?
interview.answer: A computed property name is an object-literal key written as [expression]. JavaScript evaluates the expression and uses its result as the property name.
interview.followUp: How would you create a key named mobileSize from size? Use a template literal such as [`mobile${param.charAt(0).toUpperCase()}${param.slice(1)}`].

interview.question: How is the expression in a computed object key used?
interview.answer: The expression is placed inside square brackets, for example {[items]: "Hello"}. The resulting value becomes the key, so an array used there is converted to its property-key representation.
interview.followUp: What key does {["A", "B"]: 1} create? The array is converted to the string "A,B", so the resulting key is "A,B".

interview.question: When would you choose a computed property name?
interview.answer: Computed names are useful when an object must derive keys from variables or expressions rather than fixed identifiers. They provide the object-literal equivalent of dynamically selecting a property name.
interview.followUp: How can a computed name be used for a method? Write [expression](parameters) {} inside the object initializer.

keyPoints: Object literals support keys whose names are calculated rather than written as fixed identifiers.
Write the key expression between square brackets immediately before the colon or method definition.
The expression’s evaluated result becomes the object property key.
The notation resembles bracket property access because both use square brackets for dynamic names.
The same dynamic-key idea used for property access is available directly while constructing an object.
An expression can be an array or another value-producing expression, not only a simple variable.
gotchas: Computed property names belong to JavaScript object initializers, not JSON syntax; JSON does not permit them.

Currying.summary: Currying transforms a multi-argument function so it can be called through successive calls such as `f(a)(b)(c)`. The wrapper collects arguments and invokes the original function when enough have been supplied.
Currying.explanation: Currying transforms a function that accepts several arguments together into one that can receive them through successive calls. A wrapper stores previously received arguments and invokes the original function once the required count is available.

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: The function to transform into a curried callable.

Currying.returns: A wrapper function that accepts arguments incrementally and calls the original function after receiving enough arguments.

example.title: Curry a function
example.explanation: This implementation collects arguments until it has enough to invoke the original function, supporting both chained and mixed calls.

useCases.title: Create reusable partial functions
useCases.scenario: Build specialized functions by pre-supplying some arguments.

useCases.title: Chain function calls
useCases.scenario: Compose data-processing or configuration pipelines.

useCases.title: Handle staged inputs
useCases.scenario: Adapt APIs that provide values one at a time.

keyPoints: Currying changes a function's calling form rather than changing the operation it performs.
A multi-argument call can be represented as a sequence of one-argument calls.
The curry operation returns a transformed wrapper; the original function runs only after enough arguments arrive.
The helper returns a wrapper that begins collecting arguments for the original function.
Each partial call can retain earlier arguments through a closure.
gotchas: Creating a curried function changes how it can be called; it does not execute the original function immediately.
A practical JavaScript curry helper may support supplying all arguments at once as well as providing them in stages.

Date parsing.summary: Date.parse(str) reads a date from a string and returns its timestamp in milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC. Invalid formats produce NaN.
Date parsing.explanation: Date.parse(str) interprets a date string and returns the corresponding timestamp: the number of milliseconds since 1 January 1970 in UTC. It accepts the full date-time form or shorter year, year-month, and year-month-day forms; an invalid format produces NaN.

parameters.name: str
parameters.description: A date string in the documented date-time format or one of its shorter variants.

Date parsing.returns: A timestamp: the number of milliseconds from 1 January 1970 UTC+0, or NaN for an invalid format.

example.title: Parse an ISO-style date string
example.explanation: Parses a date-time string with an explicit offset and prints its millisecond timestamp.

useCases.title: Normalize date input
useCases.scenario: Convert an API date string into an epoch-millisecond value for comparison or storage.

useCases.title: Build a Date object
useCases.scenario: Create a Date instance from a parsed timestamp when date methods are needed.

useCases.title: Check parsing success
useCases.scenario: Validate a date string before accepting it in application input.

interview.question: What does Date.parse return?
interview.answer: Date.parse(str) converts a supported date string into a numeric timestamp measured in milliseconds from 1 January 1970 UTC. It returns NaN when the format is invalid.
interview.followUp: How would you safely use the result? Check Number.isNaN(timestamp) before constructing a Date or performing calculations.

interview.question: What string format does Date.parse accept?
interview.answer: The documented full form is YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ. T separates the date and time, the fractional seconds are optional in shorter forms, and Z or a numeric offset supplies time-zone information.
interview.followUp: What shorter inputs are supported? YYYY, YYYY-MM, and YYYY-MM-DD are documented shorter variants.

interview.question: What is the meaning of the returned number?
interview.answer: A valid parsed value is a timestamp, meaning milliseconds counted from 1 January 1970 at UTC+0. This numeric result can be passed to the Date constructor to create a Date object.
interview.followUp: What should happen for malformed input? Treat NaN as invalid rather than as a usable timestamp.

keyPoints: Date.parse takes one string argument and interprets it as a date.
The complete documented pattern combines a calendar date, a T separator, a time, optional fractional seconds, and zone information.
T divides the date portion from the time portion.
A numeric offset such as -07:00 identifies the offset from UTC.
The parser also permits date-only strings with reduced precision.
Successful parsing produces an epoch-millisecond number rather than a Date object.
gotchas: Parsing failure does not throw an exception; Date.parse returns NaN, so check with Number.isNaN before using the result.
The standalone Z designates UTC+0, while a numeric offset expresses a different time zone.

Debounce.summary: debounce(f, ms) returns a wrapper that waits until calls stop for ms milliseconds, then invokes f once with the latest arguments. New calls cancel the previous scheduled invocation.
Debounce.explanation: Calling debounce returns a wrapper. Each wrapper call cancels the previous timer and starts a new one, so the original function runs only after ms milliseconds without another call, using the latest arguments and preserving the caller's this value.

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: The function whose calls are delayed and coalesced.

parameters.name: ms
parameters.description: The inactivity interval in milliseconds.

Debounce.returns: A wrapper function that delays invocation of f.

example.title: Trailing-edge debounce
example.explanation: The first two calls are superseded; after the final call in each burst, the wrapped function runs once.

useCases.title: Text-input processing
useCases.scenario: Run a search or validation only after the user pauses typing.

useCases.title: Mouse-movement processing
useCases.scenario: Handle the final pointer position after movement stops.

useCases.title: Event-burst consolidation
useCases.scenario: Coalesce a burst of events when intermediate states do not need processing.

interview.question: What does debounce do?
interview.answer: A debounced wrapper postpones the original call until the specified quiet period has elapsed. Every new wrapper call cancels the previous timeout, and only the final call's arguments reach the original function.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve the receiver? Use a normal function wrapper and invoke the target with func.apply(this, args), rather than using an arrow wrapper that captures the wrong this.

interview.question: When does the wrapped function execute?
interview.answer: The timeout is reset after every invocation of the wrapper. Therefore, a continuous stream of calls keeps postponing execution; the wrapped function runs once only after the stream stops for ms milliseconds.
interview.followUp: What happens if calls never stop? The trailing invocation may never occur, because the required inactivity interval is never reached.

interview.question: How does debounce differ from throttle?
interview.answer: Debounce suits event sequences such as key presses or mouse movement when only the final state should be processed. Throttle is different: it runs no more often than the specified interval and is useful for regular updates.
interview.followUp: Which should handle continuous scrolling updates? Usually throttle, when periodic updates are needed; debounce is better when processing the eventual final result.

keyPoints: The decorator returns a new callable wrapper instead of modifying the original function directly.
Execution is delayed until the wrapper has received no calls for the configured duration.
A burst of calls produces one trailing invocation, and that invocation receives the newest arguments.
Each wrapper invocation schedules the target for a later timer-based call.
A subsequent invocation clears the earlier timer before creating its replacement.
It is useful when an event sequence should be handled after activity has settled, such as input or pointer movement.
gotchas: Only the latest arguments are used; earlier calls in the same quiet-period window are discarded.

Deep vs Shallow Copy.summary: A shallow copy creates a new outer object but keeps references to nested objects. A deep copy recursively duplicates nested properties; `structuredClone` is the documented built-in for this purpose.
Deep vs Shallow Copy.explanation: JavaScript object assignment and ordinary copy operations preserve references to nested objects. A shallow copy creates a new outer object but shares nested objects; structuredClone creates a separate copy including nested properties, so later nested mutations do not cross between the values.

example.title: Shallow versus deep copy
example.explanation: The spread copy duplicates only the outer object, while structuredClone recursively copies supported nested values.

useCases.title: Shallow state updates
useCases.scenario: You need a new top-level object while intentionally sharing nested state.

useCases.title: Deeply isolated data
useCases.scenario: You need independently mutable nested configuration or application state.

useCases.title: Safe data handoff
useCases.scenario: You need to pass cloneable structured data across boundaries without sharing nested references.

interview.question: What is the difference between assigning an object and making a shallow copy?
interview.answer: Object variables hold references, so assignment copies the reference rather than duplicating the object. A shallow copy creates a new outer object while nested objects remain shared.
interview.followUp: What happens if a nested property is mutated through the shallow copy? The original changes too because both copies reference that nested object.

interview.question: How does structuredClone provide a deep copy?
interview.answer: structuredClone recursively clones the object and its nested properties. The resulting object can be changed without changing the original, provided its contents are supported by the structured-cloning algorithm.
interview.followUp: Why is JSON serialization not a general replacement? It is limited to JSON-representable data and can lose or transform values outside that format.

interview.question: When is a shallow copy sufficient?
interview.answer: Primitive values are copied as values, but object values are references. Therefore, a shallow copy is independent only for properties whose values are primitives.
interview.followUp: How can you test whether nested state is shared? Compare the nested references with strict equality, such as `copy.child === original.child`.

keyPoints: Objects are reference-based, whereas primitive values are copied independently.
An object variable stores a reference to the object rather than the object data itself.
Copying nested objects recursively is deep cloning, also called structured cloning.
Use structuredClone when an independent copy of nested, supported data is required.
Shallow copies isolate the top-level container but preserve references inside it.
gotchas: Assigning an object variable to another variable does not clone the object; both variables refer to the same object.
Object.assign and spread syntax copy only the outer level, so nested objects remain shared.
structuredClone is the documented deep-copy option, but it supports only cloneable values.

default parameter scope.summary: Default parameter initializers run in their own scope, outside the function body. Earlier parameters are visible, but declarations in the body are not and can cause a runtime ReferenceError.
default parameter scope.explanation: A default parameter initializer is evaluated when its argument is omitted or undefined. Initializers have a separate scope outside the function body: earlier parameters are available, but body declarations are not, so referencing one raises ReferenceError.

example.title: Default parameter scope
example.explanation: The initializer cannot access declarations in the function body, so calling greet without an argument throws ReferenceError.

useCases.title: Dependent defaults
useCases.scenario: Derive a missing argument from a preceding parameter, such as constructing a label from an earlier value.

useCases.title: Diagnosing scope errors
useCases.scenario: Recognize why a helper declared inside the body cannot be called from a parameter fallback.

interview.question: What scope do default parameter initializers use?
interview.answer: Default parameter initializers run in a scope separate from the function body. That scope is the parent of the body scope, so body declarations are not visible while an initializer is evaluated.
interview.followUp: Can an initializer use an earlier parameter? Yes. Parameters are processed left to right, so an earlier parameter is available to a later initializer.

interview.question: Can one default parameter depend on another?
interview.answer: Yes, an initializer may refer to parameters declared earlier in the parameter list. Parameters are initialized from left to right, making those earlier bindings available.
interview.followUp: What happens if it refers to a later parameter? The later parameter has not been initialized yet, so the reference fails during evaluation.

interview.question: Why can a body function not be used in a default initializer?
interview.answer: A function or variable declared in the function body cannot be referenced by a default initializer. Such a reference causes a runtime ReferenceError, including references to var declarations.
interview.followUp: Can the initializer call a function declared outside the function? Yes, outer-scope bindings remain accessible through normal lexical scope lookup.

keyPoints: Default initializers execute in a dedicated scope positioned outside the function body's scope.
A parameter may use an earlier parameter as its fallback value.
Function-body declarations are not visible from parameter initializers.
Using an inaccessible body declaration in an initializer produces a runtime ReferenceError.
The initializer is evaluated when the function is called, rather than when the function is defined.
gotchas: Declarations in the function body are unavailable to default initializers, including function declarations and var variables; referencing them throws ReferenceError.
The initializer scope is distinct from and parent to the function-body scope, which explains why body declarations cannot be reached.

Double negation.sourceTitle: Logical operators - The Modern JavaScript Tutorial
Double negation.summary: Double negation (`!!`) converts any JavaScript value to a boolean primitive using its truthiness. It is equivalent to `Boolean(value)`.
Double negation.explanation: The first ! converts a value to a boolean and reverses it; the second ! reverses that boolean again. The result is therefore the ordinary truthiness conversion, equivalent to Boolean(value), producing only true or false.
Double negation.returns: A boolean primitive: true or false.

example.title: Convert values with double negation
example.explanation: Applying ! twice converts each value to its boolean equivalent.

useCases.title: Create a boolean flag
useCases.scenario: Normalize an optional or mixed-type expression before storing or passing a flag.

useCases.title: Booleanize an operand
useCases.scenario: Convert a value while composing a larger logical expression that expects a boolean operand.

useCases.title: Expose truthiness
useCases.scenario: Make a value's truthiness explicit in a compact expression.

interview.question: What does !!value do?
interview.answer: Double negation uses two logical NOT operations: the first converts the operand to a boolean and inverts it, while the second inverts that result. The final value is therefore true or false according to the operand's truthiness.
interview.followUp: How can the same conversion be written without !!? Use Boolean(value), which performs the direct boolean conversion.

interview.question: Which values become false with double negation?
interview.answer: Falsy values such as 0, an empty string, null, undefined, and NaN become false; other values become true. Thus !!value reflects JavaScript's boolean-conversion rules rather than preserving the original type.
interview.followUp: What about the string "0"? It is non-empty, so it converts to true.

interview.question: What is the syntax and precedence behavior of double negation?
interview.answer: The expression is written as !!value. Since logical NOT has high precedence, a chain such as !!value && other is evaluated as (!!value) && other.
interview.followUp: How can precedence be made explicit? Add parentheses, for example (!!value) && other.

keyPoints: Write !!value when an expression must be normalized to the primitive boolean true or false.
Each ! is unary, so double negation consists of two unary operations applied in sequence to one value.
The first ! performs the conversion step before producing its inverted result.
Applying the second ! cancels the inversion while retaining the boolean conversion.
gotchas: Because ! has higher precedence than && and ||, each negation is evaluated before those logical operators.
The first negation does not preserve the original value: it first applies boolean conversion and then returns the opposite boolean.

Dynamic this.summary: JavaScript's regular-function `this` is determined by how the function is called, not where it is defined. Method calls provide the receiver, while standalone calls, explicit binding, constructors, and arrow functions follow different rules.
Dynamic this.explanation: For a regular function, this is supplied by the call rather than fixed by where the function was written. A method call such as obj.method() supplies obj; detaching the method removes that receiver. Arrow functions do not provide their own this and instead capture it lexically.

example.title: Invocation determines this
example.explanation: The same regular function receives different this values because it is called in different ways.

useCases.title: Reusable object methods
useCases.scenario: A shared method needs to operate on whichever object calls it.

useCases.title: Stable callback context
useCases.scenario: A callback must preserve a particular receiver after being passed elsewhere.

useCases.title: Explicit invocation control
useCases.scenario: The same function must run with different receivers or argument lists.

interview.question: How is this determined for a regular function?
interview.answer: For a regular function, this is determined at runtime by invocation. In obj.method(), it is obj; in a standalone call, it is undefined in strict mode and usually the global object otherwise.
interview.followUp: How can a method retain its receiver when passed as a callback? Use bind to create a function whose this binding does not change.

interview.question: How does arrow-function this differ from regular-function this?
interview.answer: An arrow function does not have its own this binding. It uses the surrounding lexical this, so calling it as an object method does not make the object its this value.
interview.followUp: What is a practical alternative when a callback needs the object as this? Use a regular function and bind the desired receiver, or call it through that object.

interview.question: How can this be explicitly controlled?
interview.answer: call and apply can explicitly provide this for one invocation, while bind creates a new function with a fixed this binding. These mechanisms are useful when a function is reused with different objects.
interview.followUp: What happens if the same regular function is accessed through another object? Its this value changes to the object used for that call.

keyPoints: In a method call, this lets one method implementation read or modify the receiver object.
The object immediately before the method in the call supplies the regular function's this value.

Detaching a method can change this to undefined in strict mode or to the global object in non-strict mode.

interview.question: What is the difference between == and ===?
interview.answer: == permits type conversion, so values such as 0 and false can compare equal. === requires matching types and equal values without conversion.
interview.followUp: How can NaN be tested reliably? Use Number.isNaN(value) for a type-safe NaN check, or Object.is(value, NaN) for the comparison semantics described by the page.

interview.question: How are null and undefined compared?
interview.answer: null == undefined is true, while both values compare unequal to other values under loose equality. This is a special case in the comparison rules.
interview.followUp: What does null === undefined return? false, because strict equality rejects operands of different types.

interview.question: When is Object.is() different from ===?
interview.answer: The equality table distinguishes strict equality from Object.is(). Object.is() treats NaN as equal to itself and distinguishes -0 from +0, unlike ===.
interview.followUp: What does Object.is(-0, +0) return? false, because Object.is uses SameValue semantics for those numeric values.

Loose equality can convert operands before deciding whether they match.
For ordinary numbers, equality requires the same numeric value and excludes NaN.
The table includes special behavior for NaN and signed zero.
Reversing the operands of == does not change its result.

Event loop.summary: The event loop coordinates JavaScript's asynchronous work: it runs one macrotask, drains all microtasks, may render, and then continues with the next macrotask. This ordering explains why promise callbacks commonly precede zero-delay timers.
Event loop.explanation: JavaScript repeatedly takes the oldest macrotask, runs it to completion, drains the microtask queue, and then may render before taking another macrotask. Timers, scripts, and user events become macrotasks; promise reactions are microtasks, so they can run before a ready timer.

useCases.scenario: Breaking expensive work into chunks so input and rendering can proceed.

useCases.title: Schedule follow-up work

interview.question: What is the ordering between a timer and a resolved promise?
interview.answer: The engine takes the oldest macrotask, runs all its synchronous code, then drains every pending microtask before moving to another macrotask. Rendering may occur after that microtask phase.
interview.followUp: What happens if a microtask queues another microtask? It is processed during the same drain, before the next macrotask.

interview.question: Why does Promise.resolve().then(...) usually run before setTimeout(..., 0)?
interview.answer: A timer callback is a macrotask, while a promise reaction is a microtask. If both become ready during the same turn, the promise reaction runs after the current task and before the timer task.
interview.followUp: Does a zero-delay timer run immediately? No; it schedules a later macrotask rather than interrupting the current one.

interview.question: How can a CPU-heavy synchronous loop affect responsiveness?
interview.answer: A long synchronous task prevents the event loop from taking another task. Consequently, user events, timers, and rendering cannot be handled until that task yields.
interview.followUp: How can code yield? Split work into smaller tasks, for example by scheduling a later timer, so the event loop can process other work between chunks.

keyPoints: The event loop repeatedly waits for available work, executes it, and returns to waiting.
Tasks are handled in queue order, with older pending work selected first.
Scripts, input events, and timer callbacks are placed in the macrotask queue.
After each macrotask, the engine drains the microtask queue before proceeding.
Rendering is considered after the microtask phase, before the next macrotask when appropriate.
When no macrotask is ready, the loop sleeps until new work arrives.

Event Loop.summary: The JavaScript event loop processes macrotasks one at a time, then drains all pending microtasks before rendering and moving to the next macrotask. This ordering governs scripts, timers, user events, and Promise callbacks.
Event Loop.explanation: The event loop repeatedly takes the oldest macrotask, runs it to completion, drains every queued microtask, and then allows rendering before continuing. Timers, scripts, and user events supply macrotasks, while promise handlers and explicit microtasks use the microtask queue; this ordering explains why asynchronous callbacks do not interrupt currently running JavaScript.

example.explanation: The script task prints 1 and 4, then the promise reaction runs as a microtask, and the timer callback runs as a later macrotask.

useCases.title: Keep long work responsive
useCases.scenario: Breaking work into scheduled pieces so the browser can handle other tasks between chunks.

useCases.title: Schedule deferred execution
useCases.scenario: Choosing between a timer and a microtask for follow-up work.

interview.question: What is the execution order between macrotasks and microtasks?
interview.answer: The loop removes the oldest macrotask and executes it. It then drains the microtask queue completely, renders if needed, and waits for the next macrotask when none is available.
interview.followUp: What happens if a microtask queues another microtask? The newly queued microtask is processed in the same drain, before the next macrotask.

interview.question: Why does a resolved Promise usually run before setTimeout(..., 0)?
interview.answer: A timer callback is a macrotask, while a promise reaction is a microtask. Therefore, when both are scheduled by the same task, the promise reaction runs first after the current task ends.
interview.followUp: Would zero delay make the timer run first? No; zero delay schedules a later macrotask and does not bypass the microtask checkpoint.

interview.question: Can an event-loop callback interrupt running JavaScript?
interview.answer: The current JavaScript task runs synchronously from start to finish. The event loop does not pause it to execute a callback; callbacks are queued and considered only after the current task completes.
interview.followUp: How can asynchronous code still delay input? A continuously growing microtask queue can prevent the loop from reaching later tasks, including input handling.

keyPoints: The engine alternates between processing available work and sleeping until new work arrives.
Scripts, user events, and due timer callbacks enter a FIFO-style macrotask queue.
Loading an external script creates a task whose work is running that script.
A timer callback becomes a task only when its scheduled time has arrived.
After the microtask checkpoint, the browser may render changes before taking another macrotask.
gotchas: A long chain of microtasks can postpone rendering and later tasks, so repeatedly enqueueing microtasks can make the page unresponsive.

Exponentiation operator.summary: The exponentiation operator `**` raises a base to an exponent, including fractional exponents. It is right-associative, so chained expressions group from the right.
Exponentiation operator.explanation: The `**` operator raises a base value to an exponent. JavaScript evaluates chained exponentiation from right to left, so `a ** b ** c` means `a ** (b ** c)`; fractional exponents can express roots.
