useCases.scenario: Share methods or default values across related objects without copying them into every object.

useCases.title: Trace inheritance
useCases.scenario: Inspect how an object inherits properties during debugging or puzzle solving.

useCases.title: Control object inheritance
useCases.scenario: Create an object with a deliberate prototype, including a null-prototype dictionary.

keyPoints: Objects participate in inheritance through a prototype link.
Because prototypes are objects too, they can form a chain.
The terminal prototype is identified by having null as its prototype.
Property access first checks the receiver, then delegates to its prototype.
Use Object.getPrototypeOf to inspect an object's prototype without relying on the legacy accessor.
Object.create constructs an object with a chosen prototype.
gotchas: An object's prototype link is distinct from its constructor's prototype property; do not confuse the two.
A missing property may be searched through multiple prototypes before the lookup ends.
If no prototype supplies the property, the lookup evaluates to undefined.

Prototype Chain.summary: JavaScript resolves missing properties by walking an object's prototype chain. The chain ends at null; if no object provides the property, the result is undefined.
Prototype Chain.explanation: Each object can link to another object as its prototype. When a property is missing on the object itself, JavaScript searches that prototype, then continues through successive prototypes until it finds the property or reaches null; a missing property evaluates to undefined.

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: The object whose prototype is returned.

Prototype Chain.returns: The prototype object associated with the supplied object.

example.title: Property lookup through a prototype chain
example.explanation: The child has no own greet method, so JavaScript finds it on parent through the prototype chain.

useCases.title: Method delegation
useCases.scenario: Share methods among related objects without copying each method onto every instance.

useCases.title: Prototype inspection
useCases.scenario: Inspect an object's inheritance relationship during debugging or metaprogramming.

useCases.title: Custom object composition
useCases.scenario: Create an object that delegates property lookup to a selected parent object.

interview.question: How does property lookup use the prototype chain?
interview.answer: JavaScript first checks whether the object has the requested property. If it does not, lookup continues on the object's prototype, then on that prototype's prototype, until the property is found or the chain ends; an unsuccessful lookup produces undefined.
interview.followUp: What terminates the search? The chain terminates at an object whose prototype is null.

interview.question: How can you inspect and create prototype relationships?
interview.answer: Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) returns the object's prototype. Object.create(proto) creates a new object whose prototype is the supplied object, allowing property lookup to delegate to it.
interview.followUp: How can the relationship be inspected without relying on __proto__? Use Object.getPrototypeOf, the standard access method described by the documentation.

interview.question: Where does the ordinary object prototype chain end?
interview.answer: Object.prototype is the default prototype for ordinary object literals, and its own prototype is null. Consequently, methods such as toString can be inherited through Object.prototype.
interview.followUp: Why does an array also find object methods? Its prototype chain eventually reaches Object.prototype, where those methods are available.

keyPoints: Property access checks own properties first and then searches the prototype.
Lookup continues through every successive prototype until a match or the chain's end.
A property absent from the entire chain evaluates to undefined.
Use Object.getPrototypeOf to inspect a prototype instead of treating __proto__ as the standard API.
Object.prototype is the terminal ordinary-object prototype because its prototype is null.
Object.create establishes a chosen prototype when creating an object.
gotchas: A prototype can have its own prototype, creating a chain rather than a single fallback object.
Prototype lookup eventually stops at null; it does not continue indefinitely.
Do not confuse an object's prototype link with the prototype property found on constructor functions.

Proxy traps.summary: JavaScript Proxy traps let a handler intercept fundamental operations on a target, such as property access, assignment, deletion, calls, and construction. Traps can customize behavior or delegate transparently to the target.
Proxy traps.explanation: A proxy handler can intercept fundamental operations on a target object through named traps. Each trap receives operation-specific arguments and can implement custom behavior or delegate to Reflect.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The original object or function whose operations may be intercepted.

parameters.name: handler
parameters.description: An object containing trap methods for selected operations.

parameters.name: property
parameters.description: The property key involved in a property operation.

parameters.name: receiver
parameters.description: The object used as the receiver for get and set operations.

Proxy traps.returns: A Proxy object that forwards unhandled operations to the target and applies the handler's traps where defined.

example.title: Intercepting object operations
example.explanation: The proxy validates assignments, hides a private-looking property, and filters it from key enumeration.

useCases.title: Validation
useCases.scenario: Reject or transform invalid assignments before they reach the target.

useCases.title: Logging and monitoring
useCases.scenario: Record reads, writes, calls, or other operations for diagnostics.

useCases.title: Access control
useCases.scenario: Expose a controlled interface while hiding selected properties or operations.

useCases.title: Function and constructor interception
useCases.scenario: Add behavior to callable or constructible objects without changing their original implementation.

interview.question: What is a JavaScript Proxy and what does a handler do?
interview.answer: A proxy wraps a target and uses a handler to intercept operations such as property reads, writes, deletion, calls, and construction. The handler can handle an operation itself or forward it to the target, commonly through Reflect.
interview.followUp: How can a proxy intercept a function call? Define an apply trap with signature apply(target, thisArg, args), or use a construct trap for new.

interview.question: Which arguments do get and set traps receive?
interview.answer: The get trap runs when a property is read and receives target, property, and receiver. The set trap runs when a property is assigned and receives target, property, value, and receiver; it should return a boolean indicating success.
interview.followUp: Why pass receiver to Reflect.get or Reflect.set? It preserves the proxy as the receiver, which matters for inherited accessors and prototype-based behavior.

interview.question: What restrictions apply to proxy traps?
interview.answer: A proxy cannot freely contradict certain target invariants. For example, a set trap cannot report success while changing a non-writable, non-configurable data property to a different value; violations can produce TypeError.
interview.followUp: What other trap can affect enumeration? ownKeys controls keys returned by operations such as Object.keys, while descriptor and configurability rules still constrain the result.

keyPoints: Create a proxy with a target and a handler; accesses through the proxy can be customized without modifying the target itself.
Use get and set to customize reads and assignments, including validation, logging, access control, or computed values.
The has trap handles membership checks made with the in operator.
The deleteProperty trap intercepts deletion attempts, including deletion of properties that do not exist.
A callable proxy can intercept invocation through apply, which receives the target function, this value, and argument list.
The construct trap customizes new operations, but the proxy target must itself be constructible.

Recursion limits.summary: JavaScript engines cap the number of nested recursive calls because each call uses stack space. The exact limit varies by engine, and exceeding it can raise a maximum-stack-size error.
Recursion limits.explanation: Each recursive call creates another execution context on the call stack, so deeper recursion consumes more memory. JavaScript engines impose a runtime-dependent maximum depth; exceeding it typically raises a stack-overflow error, making iteration preferable for very deep work.

example.title: Observing the runtime limit
example.explanation: This deliberately recurses until the runtime rejects another nested call; the reported depth varies by JavaScript engine, so it is for experimentation rather than production logic.

useCases.title: Measure an environment's practical limit
useCases.scenario: Testing runtime behavior across browsers or JavaScript hosts.

useCases.title: Prefer an explicit stack when depth may be large
useCases.scenario: Processing deeply nested trees or graphs.

useCases.title: Set and validate a safe maximum depth
useCases.scenario: Designing recursive algorithms with bounded input.

interview.question: What is recursion depth, and why is it limited?
interview.answer: Recursion depth is the maximum number of nested calls, counting the initial call. Each call adds an execution context to the stack, and the engine limits how many contexts can coexist.
interview.followUp: What determines the exact limit? The JavaScript engine and its available stack configuration; code should not depend on a particular numeric threshold.

interview.question: Why can deep recursion fail even when the algorithm is logically correct?
interview.answer: A recursive call creates another execution context, which consumes memory while callers wait to resume. Consequently, sufficiently deep recursion can exceed the stack and produce a maximum-stack-size error.
interview.followUp: How would you handle very deep input? Rewrite the algorithm iteratively, often using an explicit stack or another loop-based worklist.

interview.question: Does tail recursion remove JavaScript's recursion limit?
interview.answer: Tail-call optimization can avoid retaining the caller's execution context when the recursive call is the final operation. The documentation notes that support is not universal, so it cannot generally be relied on in JavaScript.
interview.followUp: Does putting the recursive call last guarantee safety? No; the running engine must implement the optimization, and most engines do not.

keyPoints: Recursion depth counts every active nested invocation, including the first function call.
For a recursive process whose deepest active chain contains n calls, the recursion depth is n.
The limit is imposed by the runtime engine rather than defined as one universal number for all JavaScript environments.
Active execution contexts consume memory, so increasing recursion depth increases the memory needed by the call stack.
Going beyond the available stack can result in a maximum-stack-size error.
Some engines can optimize a final recursive call so the current context need not remain on the stack.
gotchas: There is no single portable recursion limit: the maximum depth depends on the JavaScript engine.
Even a tail-position recursive call is not a safe way to assume unlimited depth, because most engines do not provide the relevant optimization.

Reflect methods.summary: Reflect exposes function-based forms of interceptable object operations, with method names matching Proxy traps. It is commonly used in proxy handlers to forward the default operation after adding custom behavior.
Reflect methods.explanation: Reflect provides function forms of JavaScript's interceptable object operations. Its methods correspond to Proxy traps, so a proxy handler can add behavior and then delegate the default operation to Reflect with the same arguments.
Reflect methods.returns: Individual Reflect methods return the result of their corresponding object operation; for example, Reflect.get returns a property value and Reflect.set returns a success boolean.

example.title: Forward proxy operations with Reflect
example.explanation: The proxy logs operations, while Reflect forwards each operation to the target using the trap's matching arguments.

useCases.title: Proxy forwarding
useCases.scenario: A proxy logs, validates, or measures property reads and writes before delegating normal behavior.

useCases.title: Dynamic object operations
useCases.scenario: Code needs property access, assignment, deletion, or construction through dynamically selected operations.

useCases.title: Default semantic delegation
useCases.scenario: A proxy handler must preserve ordinary JavaScript semantics instead of reimplementing inheritance and accessors.

interview.question: What is Reflect used for?
interview.answer: Reflect is a built-in object whose static methods invoke interceptable object internal methods. Each method corresponds to a Proxy handler method, such as Reflect.get for property reads and Reflect.set for writes.
interview.followUp: How can a proxy preserve normal behavior after logging a property read? The get trap should call Reflect.get with the target, property key, and receiver.

interview.question: How do Reflect.get() and Reflect.set() map to ordinary operations?
interview.answer: Reflect.get(target, key) performs a property read as a function call, while Reflect.set(target, key, value) performs an assignment-like operation. Reflect.set returns a boolean indicating whether the update succeeded.
interview.followUp: Why pass receiver to Reflect.get or Reflect.set? It preserves the receiver used by accessor lookup and assignment, which matters when inherited getters or setters are involved.

interview.question: What does Reflect.construct() do?
interview.answer: Reflect.construct(target, argumentsList) performs the constructor operation represented by new target(...argumentsList). Reflect.construct can also receive newTarget, allowing the constructed object's prototype relationship to use a different constructor.
interview.followUp: What does newTarget change? It changes the constructor's new.target value and can make the resulting object an instance of newTarget rather than target.

keyPoints: Reflect is especially useful inside proxy traps: it lets custom behavior delegate the underlying operation without manually reproducing it.
Reflect's static method names align with Proxy trap names, making the API predictable when forwarding operations.
Reflect.get(target, key) performs a property lookup and returns the resulting value.
Reflect.set(target, key, value[, receiver]) performs assignment and returns whether the update succeeded.
Reflect.construct(target, argumentsList) invokes a constructor with a dynamically supplied argument list.
gotchas: Reflect.set() reports assignment success with a boolean instead of exposing assignment syntax's result.
Reflect does not replace Proxy; it supplies the corresponding reflective operation used to forward a trap.
Reflect methods closely mirror low-level object operations, so they still perform the operation on the supplied target.

Regex lastIndex.summary: RegExp.lastIndex records where the next search starts for global and sticky regular expressions. Successful matches advance it, while failed exec() calls reset it to 0; assigning it manually selects a starting offset.
Regex lastIndex.explanation: A global or sticky RegExp stores the position used for its next search in lastIndex. A successful exec() or test() advances it to the end of the match; a failed search resets it to 0, and you can assign a starting position yourself.

example.title: Continuing and resetting a global match
example.explanation: A global regular expression resumes each exec() call at lastIndex; assigning 0 starts over.

useCases.title: Scanning successive matches
useCases.scenario: Iterate through every match while retaining capture groups and each match's position.

useCases.title: Resume from an offset
useCases.scenario: Start a global search at a known character offset.

useCases.title: Sticky tokenization
useCases.scenario: Parse input sequentially, requiring each token to begin exactly where the previous one ended.

interview.question: What does RegExp.lastIndex represent?
interview.answer: lastIndex is the position from which the next match begins for a global or sticky regular expression. After a successful exec(), it becomes the position immediately after the matched text; after failure, it resets to 0.
interview.followUp: What happens when lastIndex is beyond the input length? exec() finds no match and resets lastIndex to 0.

interview.question: How do global and sticky regexes differ when using lastIndex?
interview.answer: With g, the engine starts at lastIndex but may continue at later positions if the pattern does not match there. With y, matching must occur exactly at lastIndex, so it is useful for position-sensitive tokenization.
interview.followUp: How would you make a sticky regex parse from a chosen offset? Assign that offset to lastIndex before calling exec() or test().

interview.question: Why can repeated regex calls produce surprising results?
interview.answer: A global regex retains its position between calls, so repeated exec() calls can iterate through successive matches. The same stateful behavior applies to test(), which also advances lastIndex.
interview.followUp: How can a reused regex avoid stale state? Set lastIndex to 0 before the new search, or use suitable string methods that do not use the regex's saved position.

keyPoints: For a global regex, each subsequent exec() begins at the saved position and then advances that position after a match.
Assigning lastIndex lets you choose the offset where the next search begins.
The sticky flag requires the match to start exactly at lastIndex instead of scanning forward.
A failed search both returns null and resets the regular expression's saved position.
test() shares the stateful lastIndex behavior of exec() for global expressions.
String-based matching methods can avoid carrying state from an earlier regular-expression operation.
gotchas: Changing lastIndex has no effect on a regular expression without the global or sticky flag.
A failed exec() returns null and clears the saved position, so code must handle the failed result before reading the match.
Reusing a global regex can make later searches begin in the middle of a string; reset lastIndex when an independent search should start at the beginning.

requestAnimationFrame.summary: requestAnimationFrame schedules an animation callback for the browser's next suitable animation opportunity. The callback receives elapsed time in milliseconds, and its returned request ID can be used to cancel the scheduled call.
requestAnimationFrame.explanation: Calling requestAnimationFrame schedules a callback for the browser's next suitable animation-and-repaint opportunity. The callback receives elapsed page-load time in milliseconds; use that timestamp to calculate motion, and call requestAnimationFrame again when another frame is needed.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: The function scheduled to run when the browser is ready for the animation opportunity; it receives elapsed page-load time in milliseconds.

requestAnimationFrame.returns: A request identifier that can be passed to cancelAnimationFrame(requestId).

example.title: Animate an element with a frame loop
example.explanation: Moves the element for one second, using the callback timestamp to calculate progress and scheduling each next frame explicitly.

useCases.title: Custom element animation
useCases.scenario: Animating DOM properties that CSS cannot handle conveniently.

useCases.title: Time-based animation
useCases.scenario: Driving a visual update loop whose progress depends on elapsed time.

useCases.title: Cancellable animation
useCases.scenario: Stopping a pending animation when it is no longer needed.

interview.question: What does requestAnimationFrame do?
interview.answer: requestAnimationFrame schedules a callback for the nearest time when the browser wants to perform animation, typically while preparing a repaint. This lets the browser coordinate JavaScript animation work with rendering.
interview.followUp: How does a continuous animation continue? The callback must schedule the next frame by calling requestAnimationFrame again, usually after updating the element.

interview.question: What argument does the callback receive?
interview.answer: The callback receives one argument: the time elapsed since page loading, measured in milliseconds. This value can also be obtained with performance.now(), so it can drive time-based progress rather than assuming a fixed frame interval.
interview.followUp: Why use the supplied time? Frame timing depends on the browser, so elapsed time keeps motion consistent when frame intervals vary.

interview.question: How can a scheduled callback be cancelled?
interview.answer: The function returns a request ID. Pass that ID to cancelAnimationFrame(requestId) to cancel the scheduled callback before it runs.
interview.followUp: When is this useful? It allows an animation to stop cleanly when its target is removed, hidden, or no longer relevant.

keyPoints: The call accepts a callback and returns an identifier for the scheduled request.
The browser chooses the suitable execution moment rather than the code forcing an exact delay.
Use the callback's millisecond timestamp to calculate animation progress.
performance.now() provides the same kind of elapsed-time reference when independently measuring animation timing.
Use this API for animations that require JavaScript control or cannot be handled effectively by CSS.
gotchas: A scheduled callback runs once; keep its returned request ID if you may need to cancel it with cancelAnimationFrame.
DOM changes made in the callback can be grouped with other animation callbacks and CSS animations, reducing repeated geometry recalculation and repaint.

rest parameters.summary: Rest parameters let a function accept any number of arguments by gathering the remaining arguments into an array. They are written with `...` before the final parameter name.
rest parameters.explanation: A rest parameter is written as three dots before the final parameter name in a function declaration. When the function runs, any arguments not assigned to earlier named parameters are collected into that parameter as a real array, so array methods can be used directly.

parameters.description: Named parameters before the rest parameter receive their corresponding arguments.

parameters.name: ...rest
parameters.description: The final rest parameter receives all remaining arguments in an array.

rest parameters.returns: The page does not specify a general return value; the function's own return statement determines its result.

example.title: Collecting arguments with a rest parameter
example.explanation: The rest parameter gathers all arguments after the function's named parameters into an array.

useCases.scenario: A function must accept a variable number of numeric inputs.

useCases.title: Argument forwarding
useCases.scenario: A wrapper forwards an arbitrary number of arguments to another function.

useCases.title: Flexible collection processing
useCases.scenario: A utility needs direct access to array methods while processing extra inputs.

keyPoints: Arguments are gathered into one array rather than being exposed as separate named parameters.
Functions can receive more arguments than their explicitly named parameters; a rest parameter captures the extras.
Use rest parameters when designing variadic functions whose input count is not fixed.
The meaning of `...` depends on its position: at the end of a function parameter list, it is rest syntax.
gotchas: A rest parameter must be the function's final parameter; placing another parameter after it is invalid.

Set uniqueness.sourceTitle: Map and Set - The Modern JavaScript Tutorial
Set uniqueness.summary: A Set is a collection of values without keys where each value appears at most once. It is useful for membership checks and removing duplicates.
Set uniqueness.explanation: A Set stores values without keys and enforces uniqueness: adding a value already present has no effect. It can be initialized from an iterable, queried with has(), and converted back to an array when needed; iteration follows insertion order.

parameters.name: iterable
parameters.description: An optional iterable whose values are copied into the new Set.

Set uniqueness.returns: A Set object containing unique values from the optional iterable.

example.title: Remove duplicate values with Set
example.explanation: Constructing a Set from an iterable keeps each value only once, so spreading it back into an array removes duplicates.

useCases.title: Deduplicate arrays
useCases.scenario: Remove repeated primitive values from incoming arrays or user-provided lists.

useCases.title: Fast membership tracking
useCases.scenario: Track whether identifiers, permissions, or tags have already been seen.

useCases.title: Enforce uniqueness
useCases.scenario: Maintain a collection that must not contain repeated entries.

interview.question: What is the defining property of a Set?
interview.answer: A Set is a collection of values rather than key-value pairs, and each value can occur only once. It is useful when membership and uniqueness matter more than indexed access.
interview.followUp: How can an array be deduplicated? Construct a Set from the array and spread or convert that Set back into an array.

interview.question: How does new Set(iterable) initialize a Set?
interview.answer: The constructor accepts an iterable, commonly an array, and adds its elements to the new Set. Duplicate elements are therefore retained only once.
interview.followUp: What happens if no iterable is supplied? The constructor creates an empty Set.

interview.question: In what order are Set values iterated?
interview.answer: A Set can be traversed with for...of or forEach(), and its values are visited in insertion order. This preserves the order in which distinct values were successfully added.
interview.followUp: Which operation checks membership without modifying the collection? Use set.has(value), which returns a boolean.

keyPoints: Set is designed for collections of unique values and does not associate each value with a separate key.
Pass an iterable to the constructor to populate a Set immediately; an array is a common source.
Use has(value) for a boolean membership test without changing the Set.
clear() empties the entire collection in one operation.
The size property gives the number of values currently held by the Set.
gotchas: Calling add() again with an existing value leaves the Set unchanged, although add() still returns the Set itself.

useCases.title: Keep long work responsive

Short Circuit Evaluation.summary: Short-circuit evaluation makes JavaScript stop evaluating a logical expression as soon as its result is determined. The || operator stops at a truthy value, while && stops at a falsy value, and each returns the operand where it stopped.
Short Circuit Evaluation.explanation: JavaScript evaluates logical operators from left to right. With ||, evaluation stops at the first truthy value; with &&, it stops at the first falsy value. The operator returns the operand where evaluation stopped, so the result does not have to be a Boolean.
Short Circuit Evaluation.returns: The operand at which evaluation stops; with || this is the first truthy value or the last operand, and with && it is the first falsy value or the last operand.

example.title: Short-circuiting with || and &&
example.explanation: The right side of each logical expression runs only when the left side cannot determine the result.

useCases.title: Fallback values with ||
useCases.scenario: Choose a fallback when a value may be falsy.

useCases.title: Conditional execution with &&
useCases.scenario: Run an action only when a condition is truthy.

useCases.title: Guarding work
useCases.scenario: Avoid evaluating unnecessary expressions or side effects.

interview.question: How does short-circuit evaluation work for || and &&?
interview.answer: The operands are evaluated from left to right. For ||, JavaScript returns immediately when it finds a truthy operand; for &&, it returns immediately when it finds a falsy operand.
interview.followUp: What does `0 || 42` return? It returns 42, because 0 is falsy and evaluation continues to the right operand.

interview.question: Do logical operators always return Booleans?
interview.answer: Logical operators return one of their operands rather than converting the result to true or false. Thus, `"hello" || "fallback"` returns `"hello"`, while `"" || "fallback"` returns `"fallback"`.
interview.followUp: How can a Boolean result be forced? Apply Boolean conversion, such as `Boolean(value)`, or use `!!value`.

interview.question: Why can short-circuiting be useful beyond choosing a value?
interview.answer: The right operand is skipped when the left operand already determines the result. This makes expressions such as `condition && action()` useful for conditional execution, because `action()` runs only when `condition` is truthy.
interview.followUp: What happens with `a || b && c`? && has higher precedence, so it is grouped as `a || (b && c)`; parentheses can make that grouping explicit.

keyPoints: The || operator evaluates operands until it encounters a truthy value, then stops.
When every earlier operand is falsy, the final operand becomes the returned value.
An expression on the right of || is skipped when the left side is truthy.
gotchas: The ! operator binds more tightly than && and ||; use parentheses when combining operators if the intended grouping is not obvious.
A function call on the right side of || or && may never happen, so side effects must not be required unconditionally.

Spread vs Rest.summary: Rest parameters gather remaining function arguments into an array, while spread syntax expands an iterable into separate arguments or elements. Both use `...`, but their syntactic position determines which behavior applies.
Spread vs Rest.explanation: The same three-dot notation has opposite roles depending on where it appears: in a function parameter list, rest gathers remaining arguments into an array; in a call or similar expression, spread expands an iterable into separate arguments or elements.

parameters.name: rest
parameters.description: The parameter name after `...`; it receives the remaining arguments as an array.

Spread vs Rest.returns: A rest parameter produces an array containing the remaining arguments; spread syntax supplies iterable items as arguments or literal elements.

example.title: Gather and expand values
example.explanation: The function gathers extra arguments into an array, while the later call expands an iterable into individual arguments.

useCases.title: Variadic functions
useCases.scenario: A function needs to accept an arbitrary number of arguments and process them as an array.

useCases.title: Forwarding iterable values
useCases.scenario: An existing array must provide individual arguments to a function call.

useCases.title: Building collections
useCases.scenario: Values from an iterable need to be inserted into an array or combined with other literal elements.

interview.question: How do rest parameters differ from spread syntax?
interview.answer: Rest parameters appear in a function definition and collect all remaining arguments into an array. Spread syntax appears in a call or similar expression and expands an iterable into separate arguments or elements.
interview.followUp: What happens if a rest parameter is followed by another parameter? It is invalid because the rest parameter must be last.

interview.question: Why use a rest parameter?
interview.answer: A rest parameter lets one function accept any number of arguments while providing those extra values as a real array. This is more convenient for array operations than an array-like argument collection.
interview.followUp: How would you pass the collected values to another function expecting separate arguments? Use spread syntax at the call site, such as `target(...values)`.

interview.question: How can an array be passed to a function that expects separate arguments?
interview.answer: Spread syntax expands an iterable in a function call, so an array can supply individual arguments to a function such as `Math.max`. The same notation can also expand values into array or object literals as documented on the page.
interview.followUp: What determines whether `...` gathers or expands? Its syntactic position: parameter-list position means rest, while call or similar expression position means spread.

keyPoints: A function parameter prefixed with `...` gathers the remaining supplied arguments into an array.
Rest is a collecting operation: values not assigned to earlier parameters are placed into one array.
Rest and spread share notation but perform inverse operations, so their position in the syntax determines the meaning.
Inside a function declaration's parameter list, trailing `...name` identifies a rest parameter.
At a call site, spread supplies the iterable's items as separate argument positions.
Rest parameters are useful for variadic functions whose callers may provide different argument counts.
gotchas: A rest parameter cannot precede another parameter; it must be the final parameter in the function definition.
Spread in a function call requires an iterable value, such as an array; it does not mean that every object can be expanded there.

Strict Mode.summary: Strict mode is enabled with the "use strict" directive at the top of a script or function. It changes JavaScript to a stricter execution mode; classes and modules enable it automatically.
Strict Mode.explanation: Strict mode is enabled by placing the exact directive "use strict" at the beginning of a script or function. A script-level directive affects the whole script, while a function-level directive affects only that function. Classes and modules enable strict mode automatically.

example.title: Strict mode rejects accidental globals
example.explanation: The strict function throws instead of silently creating a global variable.

useCases.title: Script-wide validation
useCases.scenario: Enable stricter checks in a traditional script.

useCases.title: Function-scoped strict mode
useCases.scenario: Constrain legacy code to a stricter function body.

useCases.title: Automatic strict mode
useCases.scenario: Use classes or modules without adding a directive.

keyPoints: Use the exact string directive to opt a script into strict mode.
At script level, the directive applies to the entire script.
Placing the directive at the beginning of a function limits strict mode to that function.
Classes and modules activate strict mode automatically, so an explicit directive is unnecessary there.
Strict mode is one-way for the current execution context.
gotchas: The directive must appear at the top of the script; code before it can prevent strict mode from being enabled.
Strict mode cannot be turned off once execution has entered it.

String coercion.summary: String coercion converts a value to text when JavaScript needs its string form. It happens implicitly in suitable operations or explicitly with String(value).
String coercion.explanation: JavaScript converts a value to text when an operation needs a string, such as displaying it. This conversion can happen implicitly, or explicitly with String(value). Common values receive predictable textual forms: booleans become "true" or "false", null becomes "null", and numbers become their textual representation.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value whose textual representation is required.

String coercion.returns: A string representation of the supplied value.

example.title: Explicit and implicit string conversion
example.code:
let value = true;
console.log(String(value)); // "true"
console.log(String(null));  // "null"
console.log("" + 1 + 2);   // "12"
example.explanation: Use String(value) when an explicit string conversion is intended; concatenation can produce different results because + handles strings and numbers differently.

useCases.title: Output formatting
useCases.scenario: Displaying a value through an API or output operation that requires text.

useCases.title: Explicit normalization
useCases.scenario: Making the conversion intent explicit before storing or passing textual data.

useCases.title: User-facing messages
useCases.scenario: Converting booleans or null into predictable text for labels or messages.

interview.question: When does string coercion occur, and how can it be requested explicitly?
interview.answer: String coercion occurs when JavaScript needs the string form of a value, such as while displaying it. It can also be requested explicitly with String(value).
interview.followUp: What does String(false) return? It returns the string "false", not the boolean false.

interview.question: What are the results of converting a boolean and null to strings?
interview.answer: String(true) produces "true", and String(null) produces "null". The result is a string even though the inputs have different types.
interview.followUp: How would you verify the result type? Apply typeof to the converted value; it returns "string".

interview.question: Why should explicit String(value) be preferred when text is required?
interview.answer: String conversion is distinct from numeric conversion: String(value) creates textual output, whereas arithmetic operators may convert operands to numbers. Use String when the required result is a string.
interview.followUp: What happens when a string is passed to Number instead? A numeric string can become a number, while an invalid numeric string becomes NaN.

keyPoints: Operators and functions may perform implicit conversion when their required input type differs from the supplied value.
String coercion supplies a value's textual representation when an operation needs text.
Use String(value) for an explicit conversion instead of relying on an operation to infer the desired type.
Boolean false and null convert to the literal strings "false" and "null".
String conversion is one of JavaScript's three commonly used type conversions, alongside number and boolean conversion.
gotchas: String conversion does not produce an empty string for null or booleans: null becomes "null", while false becomes "false".

String immutability.sourceTitle: JavaScript data types and data structures
String immutability.summary: JavaScript strings are immutable: once created, their contents cannot be changed. String operations return new strings, so retain the result when you need transformed text.
String immutability.explanation: A JavaScript string cannot be changed after it is created. Operations that appear to edit text instead produce another string, which you can store by assigning the returned value to a variable; the variable itself may still be reassigned.
String immutability.returns: String operations that transform or combine text return a new string; the original remains unchanged.

example.title: Create a changed string
example.explanation: replace() returns a new string, so the original value remains unchanged.

useCases.title: Text transformation
useCases.scenario: Normalize or transform user input without altering the original value.

useCases.title: String composition
useCases.scenario: Build labels, messages, or paths from existing string values.

useCases.title: Non-destructive updates
useCases.scenario: Preserve an original value while producing an edited variant.

interview.question: What does string immutability mean in JavaScript?
interview.answer: Strings are immutable primitive values, so their contents cannot be modified in place. Methods such as replace() return a new string rather than changing the receiver.
interview.followUp: What happens if a variable holds a string? The variable can be reassigned to the newly returned string, but the original string value is still unchanged.

interview.question: How can you change one character in a string?
interview.answer: An assignment such as str[0] = "H" cannot replace the first character of a string. To change the text, construct a new string and assign that new value to the variable.
interview.followUp: How would you replace every occurrence? Use replaceAll(), or use replace() with a global regular expression.

interview.question: Why must the result of a string method be assigned?
interview.answer: String transformation methods return new strings because primitive values are immutable. Therefore, code must capture the return value when it needs the transformed text.
interview.followUp: Does const make the string immutable? No: the string value is immutable independently; const only prevents rebinding that particular variable.

keyPoints: String immutability is part of the broader rule that primitive values cannot be altered in place.
Existing string contents remain fixed for their entire lifetime.
Methods that transform or extract text produce a separate string value.
Combining strings also creates a result rather than extending either operand.
The returned value is the place to find the transformed text.
gotchas: Character assignment does not modify a string; use an operation that creates a replacement string and save its result.

Symbol uniqueness.sourceTitle: Symbol type - The Modern JavaScript Tutorial
Symbol uniqueness.summary: JavaScript symbols are primitive unique identifiers. Separate Symbol() calls stay distinct even with the same description, while Symbol.for(key) reuses a symbol from the global registry.
Symbol uniqueness.explanation: Calling Symbol() creates a primitive identifier that remains distinct from every other symbol, even when descriptions match. The description is only a label. If code needs the same symbol to be retrieved repeatedly by name, use Symbol.for(), which consults the global symbol registry and creates an entry when needed.

parameters.name: description / key
parameters.description: An optional description or registry key used to label or retrieve a symbol.

Symbol uniqueness.returns: Symbol() returns a unique primitive symbol; Symbol.for(key) returns the registry symbol associated with key, creating it if absent.

example.title: Comparing ordinary and registered symbols
example.explanation: Separate Symbol() calls remain distinct, while Symbol.for() reuses a registry entry for the same key.

useCases.title: Collision-resistant object keys
useCases.scenario: Adding metadata or internal fields to objects without colliding with ordinary string property names.

useCases.title: Shared cross-module identity
useCases.scenario: Sharing one named symbol between modules or other code that uses the same registry key.

useCases.title: Stable private-style markers
useCases.scenario: Representing internal identifiers whose identity should not be recreated accidentally.

interview.question: Why are two symbols with the same description not equal?
interview.answer: Each Symbol() call produces a distinct primitive, so Symbol("x") === Symbol("x") is false. The optional description does not participate in symbol identity.
interview.followUp: How can separate parts of an application obtain the same symbol? Use Symbol.for("x"), which retrieves or creates the registry entry for that key.

interview.question: How does Symbol.for() differ from Symbol()?
interview.answer: Symbol.for(key) checks the global symbol registry and returns the existing entry for that key, creating one if necessary. Repeated calls with the same key therefore return the same symbol.
interview.followUp: What is the contrasting behavior of Symbol("x")? It creates a fresh symbol on every call, even when the description is identical.

interview.question: Why use symbols as object property keys?
interview.answer: A symbol is a primitive value used as a unique identifier, and it can serve as an object property key. This allows code to add a property without accidentally colliding with an unrelated string-named property.
interview.followUp: What should be used for cross-code shared identity? A registered symbol from Symbol.for(), accepting that its identity is intentionally shared rather than fresh.

keyPoints: Symbols provide primitive identifiers intended to remain distinct.
Every ordinary Symbol() result has unique identity.
Equal descriptions do not merge symbols; each call still yields a different value.
Symbol.for(key) provides named lookup through the global symbol registry.
The registry makes repeated requests with one key return one shared symbol.
gotchas: Matching descriptions do not make symbols equal; descriptions are informational labels only.
Use Symbol.for(key), rather than Symbol(key), when repeated lookup by a shared name must return the same symbol.

Symbol.toPrimitive.summary: Symbol.toPrimitive is a well-known symbol used to define an object's conversion to a primitive. JavaScript calls the associated method with a hint before falling back to valueOf() and toString().
Symbol.toPrimitive.explanation: When an object must become a primitive, JavaScript first checks for a method under Symbol.toPrimitive and passes it a hint: "string", "number", or "default". The method may choose how to interpret that hint, but it must return a primitive; otherwise conversion throws a TypeError. If the method is absent, JavaScript falls back to valueOf() and toString() according to the conversion context.

parameters.name: hint
parameters.description: A hint indicating the preferred primitive context: "string", "number", or "default".

Symbol.toPrimitive.returns: A primitive value chosen by the conversion hook; returning a non-primitive causes a TypeError.

example.title: Customize object conversion
example.explanation: The same object supplies different primitive representations for string and numeric contexts.

useCases.title: Context-sensitive formatting
useCases.scenario: An object should display a formatted value in string contexts but retain a raw numeric value in arithmetic.

useCases.title: Custom operator coercion
useCases.scenario: A domain object needs predictable behavior when used with operators or interpolation.

useCases.title: Controlled API conversion
useCases.scenario: A library exposes objects that should convert to a stable primitive representation.

interview.question: What is Symbol.toPrimitive used for?
interview.answer: JavaScript calls obj[Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) before the fallback methods. The hint is "string", "number", or "default", and the hook must return a primitive.
interview.followUp: What happens when the hook is missing? JavaScript uses toString() first for a string hint, and valueOf() first for number or default hints.

interview.question: What do the Symbol.toPrimitive hints mean?
interview.answer: The hook receives a preferred conversion context, but it can return any primitive representation it chooses. The returned type does not have to match the hint.
interview.followUp: Why can one object behave differently in template literals and arithmetic? Each operation supplies a different hint, which the hook can handle separately.

interview.question: How does Symbol.toPrimitive interact with valueOf() and toString()?
interview.answer: The hook has priority over valueOf() and toString(). If it exists, JavaScript uses it for all primitive conversions instead of proceeding to those fallback methods.
interview.followUp: What must the hook return? A primitive value; returning an object results in a TypeError.

keyPoints: Define a computed property using Symbol.toPrimitive to customize how an object becomes a primitive.
The hint identifies the operation's preferred context, allowing one hook to distinguish text, numeric, and general coercion.
Without the well-known-symbol hook, conversion falls back to the object's conventional conversion methods.
The hook controls string, number, and default conversions rather than applying only to one operator.
gotchas: The conversion hook is looked up using the well-known symbol key, not an ordinary string property named "Symbol.toPrimitive".
Returning an object from the hook is invalid and causes primitive conversion to fail with a TypeError.

Tail Call.summary: A tail call is a final function call with no work left for the caller. Tail-call optimization can reduce stack usage for suitable recursion, but JavaScript engine support is not universal.
Tail Call.explanation: A tail call is a function call whose result is returned immediately, with no work left for the caller. In strict-mode code, an implementation can discard the caller's execution context before invoking the target, allowing tail recursion to avoid accumulating stack frames; this optimization is not consistently available in JavaScript engines.

example.title: Tail-recursive factorial
example.explanation: The recursive call is the function's final operation, so it is in tail position. However, JavaScript engines do not all implement the optimization, so this pattern can still exhaust the call stack.

useCases.title: Tail-recursive traversal
useCases.scenario: Recursive algorithms whose recursive invocation is the final operation.

useCases.title: Accumulator-based computation
useCases.scenario: Recursion with an accumulator carrying intermediate state.

useCases.title: Execution-stack analysis
useCases.scenario: Reasoning about stack growth in recursive JavaScript code.

interview.question: What is a tail call?
interview.answer: A tail call occurs when a function call is the final action of its caller, so the caller has no computation left afterward. A tail-recursive function passes its accumulated result into the recursive call rather than multiplying or adding after that call returns.
interview.followUp: Why can ordinary recursive factorial overflow while a tail-recursive form may not? Ordinary recursion must retain each suspended caller for later work; a recognized tail call can avoid retaining those contexts, although engine support is uneven.

interview.question: What benefit does tail-call optimization provide, and is it guaranteed?
interview.answer: Tail-call optimization reduces memory pressure by avoiding storage of the caller's execution context when the recursive call is last. JavaScript engines do not universally provide this optimization, so code cannot depend on it for arbitrary input sizes.
interview.followUp: What practical alternative avoids this portability issue? Rewrite the recursion as an explicit loop, which does not consume one JavaScript call frame per iteration.

interview.question: How can you recognize whether a recursive call is in tail position?
interview.answer: In `return factorial(n - 1, n * result)`, the recursive invocation is returned directly and no arithmetic follows it, making it tail position. In `return n * factorial(n - 1)`, multiplication must happen after the recursive call returns, so that call is not tail position.
interview.followUp: What must change to make the second form iterative? Carry the partial product in a variable and update it inside a loop before decrementing the counter.

keyPoints: A recursive call qualifies for tail-call optimization when it is the function's final operation and the caller has no remaining calculation.
Because the caller has nothing left to do, the engine can avoid preserving its execution context for resumption.
Reusing or discarding the caller's context reduces memory required by deeply recursive execution.
Recursion depth is bounded by the particular JavaScript engine rather than by a universal language-wide number.
gotchas: Do not assume that tail-recursive code is stack-safe: support varies by engine and the optimization has limited applicability.
Even a recursive design that appears suitable for tail-call optimization may hit an engine-specific recursion limit.

Temporal dead zone.summary: The temporal dead zone is the interval from entering a block until execution initializes a let, const, or class binding. Accessing the binding during that interval throws a ReferenceError.
Temporal dead zone.explanation: A const binding exists throughout its block, but it remains uninitialized from block entry until execution reaches its declaration. Accessing it during that interval throws a ReferenceError; the relevant boundary is execution order, not merely the declaration’s position in the source.

interview.question: What is the temporal dead zone for const?
interview.answer: A const binding is in the TDZ from the beginning of its block until execution reaches its declaration and initialization. Reading it earlier throws a ReferenceError rather than returning undefined.
interview.followUp: Does moving the declaration text always fix the problem? No: the access must execute after initialization, so control flow and calls matter.

interview.question: Why can a function declared before const still access it?
interview.answer: The TDZ is based on execution order. A function may be defined before a const declaration and still read that binding successfully when called after the declaration has executed.
interview.followUp: What happens if the function is called before initialization? Its read occurs inside the TDZ and throws a ReferenceError.

interview.question: How does const differ from var before initialization?
interview.answer: `var` is initialized to undefined during hoisting, whereas const remains uninitialized until its declaration executes. Consequently, an early const access throws a ReferenceError.
interview.followUp: Does `typeof` avoid this error? No; applying it to a lexical binding in the TDZ also throws a ReferenceError.

keyPoints: The TDZ applies to const bindings as well as let and class bindings.
For const, the TDZ begins when its block starts and ends when its declaration runs.
The binding exists conceptually but has no usable value during this interval.
Reading the binding before initialization fails at runtime with ReferenceError.
Initialization occurs when control reaches the declaration, not merely when the script is parsed.
gotchas: `typeof` does not safely probe a lexical binding while it is in the temporal dead zone.
A function written before the declaration can still work if it is called only after initialization.

interview.question: What is the temporal dead zone?
interview.answer: A TDZ is the interval from the start of a block until execution reaches and initializes a `let`, `const`, or `class` declaration. Accessing the binding in that interval throws a `ReferenceError`.
interview.followUp: Does source position alone determine the error? No; the ordering of execution and the declaration's initialization is what matters.

interview.question: How does TDZ behavior differ from `var`?
interview.answer: `let` and `const` bindings are available only after execution reaches their declaration, so an earlier read fails. A `var` binding instead receives `undefined` when hoisted, so this particular TDZ error does not occur.
interview.followUp: What about `typeof`? It still throws for a lexical binding inside its TDZ.

interview.question: When does a TDZ end?
interview.answer: The binding is initialized when execution reaches the declaration. With `let` and no initializer, that initialization gives the variable `undefined`; with `const`, an initializer is required.
interview.followUp: Why must `const` have an initializer? It cannot be assigned later, so leaving it uninitialized would make it unusable.

keyPoints: For `let`, `const`, and `class`, the TDZ begins at block entry and ends when execution reaches the initialized declaration.
The binding exists conceptually but has no usable value during the TDZ.
Initialization happens at runtime when control reaches the declaration, not simply when the scope is created.
A `let` declaration without an initializer becomes `undefined` once execution reaches it.
The term applies to all three lexical declaration forms documented on the page.
gotchas: Reading a binding during its TDZ throws instead of producing `undefined`.
Moving execution order or calling code earlier can trigger the TDZ even when the declaration is visibly present below.

Ternary associativity.summary: JavaScript’s conditional (ternary) operator selects one of two values from a condition. Chained `?` expressions are grouped right-to-left, enabling compact multi-condition selection.
Ternary associativity.explanation: A conditional expression evaluates its condition and produces the value after `?` when truthy or after `:` otherwise. When conditional operators are chained, they group from right to left, allowing an if/else-if/else-style value selection.

interview.question: How are chained ternary expressions grouped?
interview.answer: The conditional operator is right-associative. Therefore, `a ? b : c ? d : e` groups as `a ? b : (c ? d : e)`, which supports an if/else-if/else-style chain.
interview.followUp: What does right-associative mean here? It describes implicit grouping, not that every operand is evaluated immediately; the condition determines which result expression is selected.

interview.question: What value does a conditional expression produce?
interview.answer: The condition is evaluated first. If it is truthy, the expression after `?` supplies the result; otherwise, the expression after `:` supplies it.
interview.followUp: How would you make the grouping unambiguous? Add parentheses around the intended nested conditional, especially when the expression becomes difficult to read.

interview.question: What is the ternary operator's basic syntax and purpose?
interview.answer: The syntax is `condition ? value1 : value2`. The operator has three operands: a condition and two alternative expressions.
interview.followUp: When should it be replaced with `if`? Use `if` when different branches need to perform statements rather than simply select one value.

keyPoints: The conditional operator is called ternary because it accepts three operands: a condition and two result expressions.
A truthy condition selects the first result; a falsy condition selects the second.
Chaining conditional operators lets one expression choose among several values based on multiple conditions.
Its core form places the condition before `?`, the truthy result between `?` and `:`, and the fallback result after `:`.
Use it for compact value selection when each branch is an expression.
gotchas: Nested conditional expressions are intended to choose values; use `if` when the branches need to execute different statements.
Its low precedence affects grouping with comparisons, so a comparison can be written directly as the condition.

this binding.summary: JavaScript’s `this` for regular functions comes from the call form, not the definition. Use `bind` to create a callable function with a fixed `this` and optional initial arguments.

Calling through `object.method()` makes the object the receiver; extracting the method removes that receiver, while `bind` creates a callable function with a fixed `this`. A bound function keeps the chosen context and initial arguments from the moment `bind` is called.

interview.question: What does a throttle decorator do?
interview.answer: `throttle(f, ms)` returns a wrapper that calls `f` no more than once during each `ms` interval. The first wrapper call runs `f` immediately and starts the cooldown; later calls are retained until the interval ends.
interview.followUp: How does the implementation handle calls during the cooldown? It stores the latest arguments and `this`, then invokes the wrapper with them when the timer expires.

interview.question: Describe the main state transitions in a throttle implementation.
interview.answer: The wrapper uses a boolean cooldown flag. A timer clears that flag after `ms` milliseconds and, if a call was saved, re-enters the wrapper to process the latest saved invocation.
interview.followUp: Why use a timer rather than polling? The timer schedules the transition at the end of the cooldown without repeatedly checking elapsed time.

interview.question: Why must `this` and arguments be preserved?
interview.answer: The wrapper must forward the original receiver and arguments, typically by applying the function with the saved context and argument list. Otherwise methods can lose their `this` value, and parameter data can be lost.
interview.followUp: What behavior differs from debouncing? Throttling permits regular execution during sustained calls, whereas debouncing waits for a quiet period and favors the final result.

keyPoints: The decorator accepts a function and interval, then produces a replacement function for callers to use.
Repeated calls are rate-limited so the wrapped function cannot run more often than the configured interval.
The leading invocation executes immediately and marks the wrapper as being in its cooldown period.
While throttled, incoming calls update stored invocation data instead of directly executing the target.
A timeout ends the cooldown after the requested interval.
gotchas: A correct decorator must preserve both the arguments and the receiver context when forwarding calls.
Calls made during the cooldown are not all replayed; only the most recent saved invocation is forwarded afterward.

Truthy and Falsy.summary: JavaScript converts values to Boolean in conditions and logical expressions. Most values are truthy; false, zero, the empty string, null, undefined, and NaN are falsy.
Truthy and Falsy.explanation: JavaScript converts an expression to a Boolean when it is used as a condition or with Boolean conversion. Falsy values include false, 0, -0, 0n, the empty string, null, undefined, and NaN; other values, including empty arrays and objects, are truthy.

interview.question: What are truthy and falsy values in JavaScript?
interview.answer: A truthy value is converted to true in a Boolean context, while a falsy value is converted to false. Falsy values include false, 0, -0, 0n, the empty string, null, undefined, and NaN.
interview.followUp: What does Boolean([]) return? It returns true because arrays are objects, and objects are truthy.

interview.question: How does && use truthiness?
interview.answer: The && operator evaluates from left to right and returns the first falsy operand. If every operand is truthy, it returns the last operand, preserving that operand's original value.
interview.followUp: What does 0 && "fallback" return? It returns 0 and does not evaluate the right operand because 0 is falsy.

interview.question: How does || use truthiness?
interview.answer: The || operator evaluates from left to right and returns the first truthy operand. If none is truthy, it returns the last operand, so it is commonly used to select a fallback.
interview.followUp: Why can || be unsuitable for defaulting a valid zero? Because 0 is falsy; use ?? when only null or undefined should trigger the fallback.

keyPoints: Truthiness is contextual: a value can be used directly as a condition without first being explicitly converted with Boolean().
The default rule is that values are truthy; only the language's defined falsy values convert to false.
The standard falsy set includes false, numeric zero forms, BigInt zero, the empty string, null, undefined, NaN, and the browser-specific document.all value.
An if condition, logical operator, or Boolean conversion can coerce a non-Boolean expression to a Boolean result for testing.
&& processes operands left to right and short-circuits as soon as it encounters a falsy operand.
Logical operators preserve selected operand values, which lets expressions produce data such as a fallback or a guarded result.
gotchas: Logical operators return an operand rather than necessarily returning true or false: && stops at the first falsy operand, while || stops at the first truthy operand.

Type coercion.summary: Type coercion is JavaScript's automatic or implicit conversion from one data type to another. It explains why operations such as addition may produce a string or number depending on the operands.
Type coercion.explanation: JavaScript may automatically convert a value when an operation expects another type. Primitive conversion uses the value's conversion rules, while object conversion consults Symbol.toPrimitive first and then valueOf() and toString().

interview.question: What is type coercion?
interview.answer: Type coercion is JavaScript's automatic or implicit conversion between data types. It commonly appears when an operation receives values whose types do not match the operation's expected type.
interview.followUp: How can implicit coercion be avoided? Use explicit conversions such as Number(value) or String(value), and choose operators whose behavior is clear.

interview.question: How are objects converted to primitive values?
interview.answer: For object-to-primitive conversion, JavaScript first checks Symbol.toPrimitive. If that does not provide the result, it tries valueOf() and then toString(), using an order determined by the conversion hint.
interview.followUp: What must Symbol.toPrimitive return? A primitive value; returning an object causes a TypeError.

interview.question: What does Number(value) do for common inputs?
interview.answer: Number(value) performs numeric conversion: null becomes 0, booleans become 1 or 0, undefined becomes NaN, and strings are parsed as numeric literals. A failed string parse produces NaN.
interview.followUp: What special issue applies to BigInt conversion? Converting BigInt to Number can lose precision, and Number and BigInt cannot be mixed directly in operations.

keyPoints: Type coercion changes a value's type automatically or implicitly.
Many operations accept a value of one type and convert it to the type they require.
Object-to-primitive conversion tries Symbol.toPrimitive, then valueOf(), then toString() for the default hint.
JavaScript has separate Number and BigInt numeric types.
Primitive coercion uses the default hint and follows the listed method order.
gotchas: Operations with mismatched types can silently trigger implicit conversion instead of throwing a type error.
A custom Symbol.toPrimitive method must return a primitive, not another object.

interview.question: What is type coercion in JavaScript?
interview.answer: Type coercion is the automatic conversion of a value from one type to another. JavaScript permits this because it is weakly typed, so operations can convert mismatched operands instead of immediately throwing a type error.
interview.followUp: How does object conversion begin? JavaScript first checks Symbol.toPrimitive, then falls back to valueOf() and toString() according to the conversion hint.

interview.question: Why can + produce concatenation rather than addition?
interview.answer: The + operator can concatenate when string conversion is selected, so a numeric operand may become text. Explicit Number(value) conversion makes numeric addition intentional and avoids relying on that choice.
interview.followUp: What happens with Number(null), Number(undefined), and Number(true)? They become 0, NaN, and 1 respectively.

interview.question: How are objects coerced to primitive values?
interview.answer: Object-to-primitive conversion uses Symbol.toPrimitive first. If it is absent, JavaScript tries valueOf() and toString() in the order determined by the hint.
interview.followUp: For a string hint, the order is toString() followed by valueOf(); for numeric conversion, the preferred order is Symbol.toPrimitive("number"), valueOf(), then toString().

keyPoints: JavaScript commonly accepts a value in a context requiring another type and converts it automatically.
Primitive coercion applies when an operation needs a primitive but does not strongly require string, number, or BigInt.
Numeric coercion distinguishes the Number and BigInt numeric types.
For objects, Symbol.toPrimitive is consulted before valueOf() and toString().
String conversion prefers Symbol.toPrimitive with a string hint, then toString(), then valueOf().
gotchas: Implicit conversion can make an expression use a different type than the operand visibly suggests.
With +, JavaScript can choose string concatenation instead of numeric addition when one operand becomes a string.
A custom Symbol.toPrimitive method must return a primitive, not another object.

Although it has its own type, typeof null produces the string "object" because of a historical language error preserved for compatibility, so strict equality is required for an exact null check.

interview.question: What does typeof null return, and is null an object?
interview.answer: typeof null returns the string "object". This is a historical typeof error that JavaScript keeps for compatibility, even though null has a separate type.
interview.followUp: How should null be detected? Use strict equality: value === null.

interview.question: What does null represent in JavaScript?
interview.answer: null is a special standalone value representing nothing, emptiness, or an unknown value. It is not a reference to a nonexistent object or a null pointer.
interview.followUp: What does typeof report for null? It reports "object" because of the longstanding language error.

interview.question: How is the typeof operator written, and what does it return?
interview.answer: The normal form is typeof x, and typeof(x) is also valid because the parentheses are optional. The result is a string naming the operand's type.
interview.followUp: What special result must be remembered? typeof null is "object", despite null not being an object.

The null type has exactly one value: null.
Assign null when a value intentionally means nothing, is empty, or is not yet known.
typeof does not return a type object; it returns a string naming the operand's type.
The operator accepts either the usual unparenthesized form or a parenthesized expression.
The special case is exact: evaluating typeof null yields the string "object".

Do not infer object-ness from typeof null; null remains a separate special value.
Use value === null when the code must distinguish null from actual objects.

Unary plus.explanation: Unary plus is the prefix `+` applied to one value. It leaves numbers unchanged and converts other values to numbers, using the same conversion behavior as `Number(...)`; this makes it useful when numeric input arrives as text.

interview.question: What does unary plus do?
interview.answer: Unary plus is the prefix `+` operator with one operand. It returns numeric operands unchanged and converts non-numeric operands to numbers, like `Number(...)`.
interview.followUp: What happens with `+true` and `+""`? They become `1` and `0`, respectively, because both values undergo numeric conversion.

interview.question: Why use unary plus with input values?
interview.answer: Use `+value` when a value should be coerced to a number, such as text returned from input. For example, `+"12"` produces the number `12`, whereas leaving the text unchanged can make binary `+` concatenate strings.
interview.followUp: Why does `+a + +b` work for numeric strings? Each unary plus converts its operand before the binary addition runs.

interview.question: How is unary plus different from binary plus?
interview.answer: JavaScript distinguishes unary plus from binary plus by the number of operands. Unary plus has one operand and converts it; binary plus has two operands and performs addition or string concatenation according to the operands.
interview.followUp: Which runs first in `+a + +b`? Both unary operators run before the binary addition because unary plus has higher precedence.

keyPoints: Unary plus is classified as a unary operator because it works with one operand.
The same `+` token represents either addition or unary conversion depending on whether it has one or two operands.
Non-number operands are coerced to numeric values.
The boolean `true` converts to the number `1`.
Unary plus has higher precedence than binary addition, so conversion happens first.
gotchas: It does not change an operand that is already a number.
Unary plus is concise, but it is not a different numeric-conversion algorithm from `Number(...)`.
In an expression containing both forms of `+`, unary conversion happens before addition because unary plus has higher precedence.

Variable Shadowing.summary: Variable shadowing happens when a nested scope declares a name already used outside it. With const, the inner binding takes precedence throughout the block and is inaccessible before initialization.
Variable Shadowing.explanation: A block-scoped const declaration can reuse an identifier from an outer scope. Inside the block, name lookup selects the inner binding throughout that block, including before its declaration is executed; accessing it then throws a ReferenceError because it is in the temporal dead zone.

interview.question: What is variable shadowing?
interview.answer: Shadowing occurs when an inner scope declares a variable with the same name as one in an outer scope. JavaScript resolves the inner binding first, so references in that inner scope use the inner variable.
interview.followUp: What happens before the inner const declaration? The binding already occupies the block, but remains uninitialized, so access throws a ReferenceError.

interview.question: Why can shadowing cause a ReferenceError before declaration?
interview.answer: A const declaration is block-scoped, and its name is available only after execution reaches the declaration. Before that point it is in the temporal dead zone.
interview.followUp: Why is the outer binding not used during that interval? The inner declaration reserves the name for the entire block, so lookup finds the uninitialized inner binding first.

interview.question: How does JavaScript choose between same-named variables?
interview.answer: JavaScript searches the innermost lexical environment first, then successively searches outer environments. Therefore, a same-named inner declaration hides the outer declaration within its block.
interview.followUp: Can the outer value still be accessed through the same identifier inside the block? Not while the inner binding is in scope; use a different name or restructure the scopes.

keyPoints: A const declared in braces is limited to that block.
Identifier lookup starts with the innermost lexical environment and falls back outward.
The same scope behavior described for let applies to const.
gotchas: A shadowing const affects the whole inner scope from its beginning, not only the lines after the declaration.
Reading the outer variable by the same name before the inner const declaration does not work; it raises a ReferenceError.

interview.question: What does the void operator do?
interview.answer: void evaluates its operand and always returns undefined. The operand can still perform side effects, because evaluation happens before its value is discarded.
interview.followUp: What does void (2 === "2") return? It returns undefined, after evaluating the comparison.

interview.question: What is the syntax and return value of void?
interview.answer: The operand is a JavaScript expression, and parentheses around it are optional. The operator's result is always undefined regardless of the operand's result.
interview.followUp: What does void 2 === "2" evaluate to? It is (void 2) === "2", so it evaluates to false.

interview.question: When might code use void?
interview.answer: void 0 and void(0) both produce undefined. The operator is also useful when an expression must be evaluated for its effects but its resulting value should not be used.
interview.followUp: Why can parentheses matter? They control whether void applies before or after another operator, avoiding precedence ambiguity.

Use it when evaluation should occur but the surrounding context requires an undefined result.
The parenthesized and unparenthesized zero forms are equivalent ways to create undefined.
Its return value does not depend on what the operand evaluates to.

Using void merely to obtain undefined is usually unnecessary in ordinary source code; the global undefined value is available for that purpose.
